Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I would like to begin by giving a brief explanation before I get into the real matter of privilege.
Last night in the House at about 5.58 p.m., the Minister of State and deputy leader of the government in the House of Commons moved:
That the amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-79, an act to
amend the Parliament of Canada Act, be read the second time and
concurred in.
The minister did not make a speech. A Liberal member, the member for Kingston and the Islands, immediately got up, agreed with the minister and spoke for less than 15 or 20 seconds. Then the chief government Whip got up and moved that the previous question be put.
We were fortunate that the member for Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing, our deputy House leader, was in the House. He spoke until six o'clock, at which time again the chief government Whip rose and tried to have the House speak after six o'clock to end the discussion on this matter.
That is all within the rules of the House. I do not question that, but the result of what they did affects the privileges of each and every member of the House.
As a result of the Senate amendments, which the House has not had a chance to review or debate, we are opening a credibility gap which members of the House and the public will never be able to bridge.
As a result of the Senate amendments, whether they were intended or not-

As a result of what happened last night, I and other members of Parliament cannot amend the motion. The chief government Whip got up and moved that the previous question be put.
The privilege is this. As a result of what happened, members in this House are not going to be guaranteed fair and equitable treatment and process by the legislation as it now stands. The Board of Internal Economy in the House and the committee that has the equivalent responsibility in the Senate, with its majority formed by the government, will decide when they will issue their opinions to police officers and when they will not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The difficulty I am in is this: The hon. parliamentary secretary has just said "debate" and it most certainly is debate.
What we have here is something which even the hon. member for Churchill agrees was done within the rules. The consequence may be that certain things somebody in the House might have wanted to do cannot take place at this time. That may have certain results.
It may be that a piece of legislation has moved farther than members in the House would want. The substance of that legislation is hardly something about which when the rules are followed, I can enter into a debate. What I am being asked to do by the hon. member for Churchill, it seems to me, is to say that the legislation is offensive, at least in the minds of some members, and that as a consequence of what was done, certain things will inevitably take place under the legislation if, in fact, the legislation is ever passed by the House. That is so clearly a question of debate that it puts the Speaker in very great difficulty trying to infer even a prima facie case of privilege under the circumstances.
I understand that there may be strong feelings about this bill. There are strong feelings about bills all the time in this Chamber, but we have rules. If the rules are followed, the fact that somebody does not like the consequence of the bill is not a question of privilege.
Of course, I will ask the hon. member for Churchill if he has anything further to add to what he has already said that would change my view. I must say in fairness to
all hon. members that the fact that hon. members may not like the consequences of a bill is not something that can be debated in the "guise"-I do not mean that in any sinister sense-of a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately because of what happened within the rules last night, we have a situation now where there will be two classes of MPs.
We will have a government majority on the Board of Internal Economy which will decide when unfavourable opinions will not be given to police officers.

He said: Madam Speaker, this motion, which I will read again-that this House condemn the government for implementing a debt reduction program which accepts the savings of children but fails to ensure that large, profitable Canadian corporations and wealthy individuals pay their fair share-has its origins in the disgust that many of us in this caucus, and I am sure many other Canadians, felt when we saw the other day the Minister of Finance accepting a cheque from a young child who was making his contribution to the debt reduction fund.
We feel that the Minister of Finance has really gone overboard in this case and that the entire government has gone overboard in its exploitation of children in order to help reduce the deficit.
Perhaps they could keep it down to a dull roar at the other end. We feel that the Minister of Finance, not only through his willingness to accept cheques from children in order to help bring down the deficit, but through other
Government Orders
policies which the government has implemented, had an over-all policy which is harmful to children and which neglects one of the ways in which we could bring down the deficit, and that is to have a fairer taxation system. That is what I want to concentrate on today.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the member is trying to deliver a speech and there are conversations being carried on, on all sides of the House. I think it very unfair to him. I would ask that there be some semblance of order so we can hear his speech.

Madam Speaker, normally I do not start raising my voice until I am about five minutes into a speech. I am trying to keep my blood pressure down, at least at the beginning.
To pick up where I left off, as I said, this motion has its origins in the disgust that we all felt watching the Minister of Finance on TV the other day accepting this cheque from children to help bring down the deficit.
I was at Wayoata Elementary School in my riding not so long ago to receive from a couple of students, Tanya Kessling and Dana de Boer, a copy of a song they had written about the environment. I think this is the kind of thing we should be seeking from children: their insights about the environment and the prospects for preserving Planet Earth, rather than their money to help bring down the deficit.
The money to bring down the deficit is out there. It is out there in the form of tax expenditures in the billions of dollars that this government maintains by virtue of its policies and its refusal to close the various tax breaks that exist for the big business sector.
If we pay attention to who was present at this debt reduction charade we had the other day in which these little kids were being asked by the Minister of Finance to break their piggy banks so that the minister would not have to tax the corporations, it was attended by the Business Council on National Issues, represented by Mr. D'Aquino. Mr. D'Aquino and his ilk represent a lot of people who either individually or as part of the corporations they either work for or own, pay absolutely no tax whatsoever.
They appoint them. What is wrong with that?

I hear the member for Mississauga South going on and on in the far comer there. I hope that when I am done, perhaps he will get up and have something to

March 22, 1991
Government Orders
say on the record rather than making life difficult for me when I am trying to speak on the record.
The Business Council on National Issues contains a number of companies, and I will just go over their record in the years 1988 and 1989, that made a profit and paid absolutely no tax at all or a very limited amount of taxes.
For instance, BCE Incorporated, Northwest Tel Incorporated, in 1989 had a pre-tax profit of $15.1 million and paid only $0.14 million in taxes. BP Canada in 1989 had a pre-tax profit of $6.2 million and had a credit of $1.4 million. Brascan in 1989 had a pre-tax profit of $442 million and paid only $0.3 million in taxes and in 1988 had a pre-tax profit of $262.8 million and paid no tax at all.
The list goes on. I will not bore the House with all the details of these various companies that make millions and millions of dollars. In the column which reads "taxes or credit", we find zero after zero after zero.
We find, not only with respect to these companies as companies, that individuals in Canada have been benefiting from the tax reforms brought in by the Tory government, to the extent that the number of people who made over $250,000 and paid absolutely no tax at all increased as a result of the Tory tax reform. The number of people who made over $50,000 and paid absolutely no tax at all increased as a result of the Tory tax reform. These are in the years 1988 and 1989.
I mention that in particular because the Minister of Finance is fond of accusing the NDP of using 1987 statistics which applied before the Tory tax reform, but I am using figures now which are after the Tory tax reform.
What we are referring to here is what we think is the moral flaw in the government's approach to reducing the deficit. If the Minister of Finance was serious about reducing the deficit and about distributing the burden of reducing that deficit, then we feel that some significant sacrifices should be asked of the corporate sector. This is what did not happen in the budget.
In that respect we released after the budget a list of what we called the five top loopholes we felt the Canadian government could deal with. We referred, for instance, to the interest deductibility rule, the business and entertainment tax deduction, the manufacturers and processing tax credit, the dividend tax credit, and the
capital gains exemption. All these five top loopholes, in our judgment, added up to some $6.7 billion.
There may be elements of these loopholes or tax breaks which one may want to maintain, but it is clear that there is a lot of money here which could accrue to the public Treasury if there were the willingness on the part of the government to make the same demands of the rich and the powerful in Canada as it makes upon children.
The government is fond of saying that it does not want to send the bill for the deficit to our children, and it is referring to the children of the future. It is willing, however, to send the bill for the deficit to the children of the present, but not all children; only the children of the poor.
What the government really means when it says it is not willing to send the bill for the deficit to children is that it is not willing to send it to the children of the rich and the powerful. They will continue to receive the tax breaks.
Indeed, the government only recently indicated that it is bringing in a reform in order to preserve, in its tax free status, the money put in trust, back in 1972, by a great many wealthy Canadians, presumably for their children. This was done as a result of reforms which took place at that time when money was put in certain trusts, would be there for 21 years, and then become taxable at the end of that 21-year period.
That 21-year period is coming up in 1993, and what did the Minister of Finance do just before he produced the budget in which he called for everyone to make a sacrifice? He indicated that he is going to change the rules with respect to trusts so that that tax break can continue in a way that it would not have continued if he were to leave the legislation as it is, and the people who have that money in trust could pay the tax which they have had 21 years' notice of having to pay. It is not as if this is some sort of surprise attack by the Treasury on people who have this money in trust.
If the Minister of Finance is serious about reducing the deficit, if he wants credibility when he says to Public Service workers that they have to accept the 3 per cent cap on their wages or that sort of thing, he must not continue to allow the corporate sector and wealthy Canadians to benefit from the reforms he has made in the tax system. These reforms have made the income tax
March 22, 1991

system less progressive. The reforms he is unwilling to make would collect some of that money from the corporations. If he is not willing to do that, then he should not really have the nerve to go to the Public Service sector or any other Canadian, for that matter, and say: "We want you to make a sacrifice".
It is the same hypocrisy which attended the government's attempt just before the budget to up the salaries of heads of Crown corporations by 4.2 per cent, at the same time, within days, it asked the Public Service to accept a 3 per cent ceiling. Actually 4.2 per cent does not look like that much when we consider some of the increases which have happened lately at the Bank of Canada. We have the head of the Bank of Canada, the architect of the government's fiscal and monetary policy, seeing his salaiy rise inappropriately at the same time as he is the great lecturer, telling Canadians about how they have to accept restraint.
All these things undermine the government's credibility when it comes to the question of deficit reduction.
I would be concerned about that for two reasons. First, if I thought the government were really concerned about the deficit, I would ask: "Why don't you do these things in order to beef up your credibility and therefore be able to fight the deficit better?"
What it points to is that the government is not really that concerned about the deficit. What the government is doing is using the deficit as a cover for what is really an ideological and philosophical agenda with respect to Canada's social programs and Canada's social spending.
It is using the deficit as an excuse to attack these programs because the Conservatives do not have the courage to do this in an open way. They know if they revealed what they were really up to, the Canadian people would say "no". They play upon the appropriate fear that all Canadians have of debt and they say they have to do these sorts of things. Therefore Canadians are more inclined to say: "Well, maybe that is what we have to do".
Government Orders
A study being done at Statistics Canada-we cannot get our hands on it yet-which shows that 44 per cent of the accumulated deficit owes its origins to tax expenditures, to the tax breaks which have been given to wealthy individuals and corporations going back to 1975 when the Liberals first started to turn the tax system into something which the corporate sector could use to make money instead of actually doing productive things. That is apparently what this study shows. The other 50 per cent is attributable to paying the interest on the debt which was created by that 44 per cent. Only 6 per cent is attributable to social spending.
Study after study has shown that social spending is not the cause of the deficit. It is other policies of the government that are the cause of the deficit. Yet it is the unwillingness of governments to admit that this is the problem.
Why are government members unwilling to admit that? It is because they would have to challenge their friends. Instead of taking decisions about funding that affect people and kids on the streets of Vancouver, the inner city of Winnipeg or Toronto or wherever, people they will never have to see, people who they do not run into in their ridings, in their lives and their social networks-they do not meet them at cocktail parties at the Canadian Club or the Carleton Club or any place like that-they prefer long-distance decisions which they never have to come to terms with the reality of.
If the Conservatives did the right thing, they would have to explain to their friends, the people who finance the Liberal and Conservative parties through donations and the people who are part of the social and economic elite of this country, why they are finally being asked to kick in and do their part. If they did have that kind of courage, if they were willing to say to those people "look, do we have a country or don't we have a country", it would not be unrelated to the question of national unity and the sense of whether or not we have a country.
It is hard to work up a sense of patriotism when we know there are people with money in this country who are unwilling to contribute their fair share to getting the country out of the so-called debt crisis we are in.

March 22, 1991
Government Orders
All we ask is that they contribute their fair share through the tax system. We are not advocating that instead of having kids lined up with their piggy banks we have individual businessmen and corporations lined up with cheques to give to deficit reduction programs. That is not how you fight the deficit.
You fight the deficit by having a fair tax system. We do not want to be part of this charade in which people line up to give money to the debt reduction fund. For that matter, most of the businesses, if they were to give, would find a way to make it tax deductible anyway. I believe there is such a provision. Let us not have this charade.
Let us have a fair tax system in which both the corporate sector and the rich and powerful in this country are finally asked to pay their fair share. They have not been paying their share for some time due to the growing imbalance in the tax system whereby the share paid by corporate taxation has gone way down and the share paid through income taxes has gone way up. Even that share, at the same time as it has been going up, has been becoming less progressive. It is more and more the middle class that is paying a larger share of the over-all pie that exists between the income tax and the corporate tax.
The other way of taxing is through consumption taxes, and that has also been going up. That also hit the middle class even harder than anyone else. The icing on the cake as far as consumption taxes was concerned was the goods and services tax.
Over all we have a tax system which is more and more asking ordinary Canadians to pay the bill for this country, while some people get away with the taxation equivalent of murder. Some of these large Canadian families, like the Bronfmans and others, own all kinds of companies and pay absolutely no tax at all. These people have made millions and millions through playing the tax system, through literally taking money out of the pockets of ordinary Canadian taxpayers and becoming millionaires at their expense.
When the day comes that this government and other governments are willing to ask them to prove they truly care about the Canadian community and that Canada is not just a place to make a buck, then we will know that
indeed we have the kind of community that will be able to withstand the pressures that are now on it.
One of the reasons we have the crisis that we have in this country is that we have fostered particularly over the last seven years, the attitude that a country is simply a place to make a dollar, that there is really no difference between one country or another, that the only way to measure these things is by how easy it is to make money in that particular country.
The majority of people, almost everybody that I know, do not have the mobility of capital. They cannot move their money down to the Caribbean or to the U.S. or to Europe or anywhere else. They are stuck here in Canada and they are glad they are stuck here in Canada, because they consider themselves to be Canadians. They do not consider themselves to be a bunch of parasites who are always judging one country over another to see whether that is the best place to put their money or is the best place to invest. They have a sense of community and belongingness and rootedness in their country, instead of having the kind of attitude which has been fostered over the years and which has been accelerated in the last seven years, whereby everything is to be judged on how much it helps one to make money or not make money.
Money is the root of all evil, and it is worshipped on the other side of the House. That is the root of Canada's problems.

Madam Speaker, I am going to participate in this debate, but I want to ask the hon. member to apologize for one thing he said today, because it is totally inaccurate. It has never been said by the Minister of Finance, nor has it been indicated by the Minister of Finance. The member erred, and I believe I am quoting him accurately when he said that the Minister of Finance has asked kids to break their piggy banks to help with the deficit.
The Minister of Finance never said that. The Minister of Finance has never indicated that. The Minister of Finance has never hinted at that. It is a very unfair statement that the hon. member made.
I sat very patiently listening to the hon. member's speech. He made some very good points. In my speech I hope I will be able to counter some of the things he said.
March 22, 1991

But that was a very unfair statement to make. I know what he is referring to. I will refer to that in my remarks as well. The Minister of Finance has never done that.
The Minister of Finance is trying to make sure that the kids today will not have to pay our bills down the road so that their kids have piggy banks. That is what this is all about. For the hon. member to make that statement, that accusation is totally unfair. I wish he would retract it.

Madam Speaker, I have no intention of retracting the statement. If the Minister of Finance is willing to appear on TV accepting a cheque from a young child for the purposes of reducing the deficit, then he has effectively given the message to a lot of kids that maybe this is something that they should do.
If they do not have their money in a piggy bank, well then I guess they cannot go and break it. To the extent that not all kids keep their money in piggy banks, I take it back. But to the extent that some kids do keep their money in piggy banks, that message implicitly calls upon them to do the same.
It is the Minister of Finance who should be ashamed of himself, not me, for allowing himself to be portrayed in that way and for allowing himself to appear in a context which gives that message.
While we are on this question, why do we want to ask future generations to pay for the deficit? I am asking the question: Why do we want to ask certain sectors of the current generation to pay for the deficit and not other sectors of this generation to pay for the deficit? That is the point. No one wants to leave any kind of inter-generational debt to anybody.
If we are leaving any debt to future generations, it is a debt which we are not willing to pay now on the environment, so that they have air to breath, soil to grow their food in, and water to drink. That is the shortsightedness in terms of the environmental deficit.
We are leaving them a deficit they might never ever be able to repay because we are so concerned about our fiscal deficit at this point that we are willing to cut back on the green plan and other things that we should be doing at this point. We will be leaving them a deficit in terms of social and economic malaise.
They will be paying for more police from now until doomsday if we do not start to do what needs to be done
Government Orders
in order to solve the problems in our inner cities. It is a question not of spending; it is a question of investment, where we are willing to spend the kind of money that needs to be spent now in order to avoid problems for future generations.
Where do we get that money? We get that money by creating the national sense of community and the national sense of will to go to these people and say: "Look, maybe in the best of all possible worlds you'd be able to keep your 80 per cent lunches through the business entertainment tax deduction and we could still fund medicare". But it is not the best of all possible worlds. It is a world in which we have to make choices between the $1.1 billion that goes to the business entertainment tax deduction or the $1.1 billion that the Minister of Finance took out of Established Programs Financing for medicare.
If I have to choose between having more nurses on the wards or more free lunches for the business community, I will choose the nurses every time.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the member and I have read the opposition motion that he put forward. I am very interested in what the NDP has to say.
As the premier of Ontario has learned, it is one thing to be in opposition and criticize and criticize; it is another thing to be in government. The NDP federally has not had the privilege, and probably never will have the privilege of being in government, and deservedly so.

Be it further resolved that it is the position of the NDP that any
reform of federal sales taxes must exempt essential goods and
services from taxation.

I do not know how the hon. member reads that resolution, but it is one thing to say: "we are against the goods and services tax, there should be no goods and services tax", and it is another thing to have a resolution of the NDP saying that: "essential goods and services should not be taxed". Madam Speaker, I recall Liberals at one time in Ontario saying that the NDP would never form the government, and displaying exactly the same kind of arrogance that the member just displayed with respect to the prospects of the NDP in Canada. It may well be-and I certainly hope it is-that that kind of arrogance will be rewarded with the same kind of political event it was rewarded with in Ontario.
The hon. member says we do not present any alternatives. We have been presenting alternative after alternative after alternative in this House, before the budget and certainly after the budget, outlining in questions to the Minister of Finance in finance committee, in statements that we have put out, where we think the government could find the money that it alleges it needs to raise through the goods and services tax and through cutbacks to what we regard as essential programs, like health care and post-secondary education.
The alternatives are there. If the member would care to read Hansard, he would find that we have been making the case over and over again, both in the debate on the GST and on the budget. The alternative to the GST is to have a fair taxation system, is to raise the money which is now forfeited through a variety of tax breaks and loopholes that we have outlined very clearly for the member and very clearly for the Minister of Finance. speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona for bringing this motion forward, because it does give the government an
opportunity for the government to put some facts before the House and before the people of Canada.
Many members here will be familiar with the saying: "Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it". However, today's motion makes it painfully clear to all Canadians that my hon. friends of the opposition have the same problems with history as they do with economics.
If this were 1981 or 1982, aspects of the motion before us would have been timely and true.
With a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Years of Liberal governments had put in place a tax system that invited abuse and avoidance, a tax system chock-a-block of loopholes, exclusions and exceptions. The result was that many large profitable corporations and wealthy individuals were able to avoid paying their fair share of the national tax burden.
Of course, there was another aspect of that decade-ago government that the opposition would also like Canadians to overlook. I do not think the NDP would, but the Liberals certainly would. That was a government, some of whose members still sit across the floor of the House although I do not see any of them today, which turned surging deficits and soaring debt into the favoured tools of national policy. We are living with the tragic results of that policy today.
The budget our government tabled last month works directly at getting Canada out of the current recession and back to growth ar.d j;b creation. It is also a budget that makes a crucial watershed choice about how this renewed prosperity must be not only achieved, but more importantly, sustained.
Instead of spending our way out of the recession, the budget's plan for economic recovery emphasizes controlling expenditures and reducing inflation. This is the key to the lower interest rates that will boost consumer spending and business investment to fuel growth and new jobs.
This approach, the fact that we are committed to stopping the growth of the national debt, obviously has its critics. We have heard them today. That is absolutely no surprise. After all, for nearly 20 years through the early 1980s Canadians were accustomed to a federal
March 22, 1991

government whose fiscal philosophy could be summed up in two words: charge it.
That is why in 1984, the government was handing out $1.33 in programs and services for every dollar it collected in taxes. That is why in the same year, we had the highest deficit in history: $38.5 billion. That is why our national debt had more than doubled to more than $200 billion in four short years.
The interest payments on that 1984 debt we inherited are a direct reason the federal government is in a deficit position today. It is the reason our national debt is now approaching $400 billion or about $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada.
The interest costs alone on the federal debt will eat up over $43 billion next year. That is equal to 36 cents of every tax dollar Canadians pay. It is more than the government spends on old age security, unemployment insurance, veterans' pensions and family allowance combined. That is why the February budget refuses to buy short-term recovery at the cost of a return to surging deficits and a runaway debt.
The lessons in the last 20 years make the point bluntly. This spendthrift approach only creates a vicious circle of higher inflation and interest rates leading us back inevitably to economic decline, lost jobs and lower government revenues.
Instead, we have taken a different path, based on a continuing commitment to deficit and debt control. The February budget severely restrains the cost of government, including wages and salaries for the Prime Minister and cabinet, for MPs and the federal Public Service.
It also extends the two-year expenditure control program that we introduced in 1990, including limits on the growth of transfers to provinces. It now continues through to 1994-95. The savings achieved will total more than $15 billion.
What makes this a watershed budget is that it also takes dramatic measures, including the creation of the Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund to achieve nothing less than a fundamental change in the political culture of government spending.
These interlocking measures will transform good financial management by government from the realm of promise and political will into a matter of law. They will ensure that all revenues from the goods and services tax go solely to servicing the deficit and getting that debt under control.
Government Orders
Perhaps I am being a bit unkind to today's opposition motion, because it can be read to suggest, although grudgingly, that they do recognize that debt reduction is a vital foundation for Canada's long-term prosperity and economic health. If that is so, I applaud sincerely this great transformation of the NDP. I wish the NDP had been more forthright in sharing such an historic transformation with all Canadians.
If this motion does finally recognize that we can no longer borrow our way to real recovery, it still fails to acknowledge the wide-ranging changes in the national tax system that our government has introduced over the last seven years. Last November my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue released his department's 1988 personal income tax statistics. I specifically asked my hon. friend today what year he was quoting from for the 1988 results, because these figures provide the first substantial result of the tax reform initiatives that we announced in 1987.
The two major thrusts of the reform were to lower tax rates and to broaden the tax base. Lower rates provided an incentive to work and invest, thereby raising living standards. Broadening the tax base, by removing special tax preferences, makes the tax system simpler and fairer and reduces the opportunities for tax planning and avoidance that were most often used by high-income Canadians.
As well, another key element of the reform was the conversion of personal exemptions into tax credits, many at enriched values, such as the child tax credit.
Unlike exemptions which provide the greatest benefit to higher income earners, credits are fairer because they provide the same degree of tax relief to all taxpayers. The results released last year showed that, as we promised, the tax system has become more progressive and the burden of taxation was reduced for most Canadians, especially for those with lower to moderate incomes.
For example, the figures released revealed the following facts. The share of total personal income tax burden paid by those earning less than $15,000 a year was reduced by almost two-thirds, from 2.1 per cent of all income tax collected in 1987 to .8 per cent in 1988, a very dramatic drop. The share of total federal income tax revenues paid by Canadians with incomes between $15,000 and $30,000 declined from 26.5 per cent to 23.1 per cent. For those earning between $30,000 and $50,000,

March 22, 1991
the share of total tax revenues dropped from 37.3 per cent in 1987 to 35.7 per cent in 1988.
By contrast, despite a larger proportional reduction in their tax rates, tax revenues from individuals with incomes between $50,000 and $100,000 increased by over 25 per cent, while tax revenues from people with incomes over $100,000 increased by 31 per cent. That is exactly what tax reform was designed to do.
I also want to highlight that the number of seniors paying income tax decreased by almost 300,000 taxpayers between 1987 and 1988. This represented an increase of 43.2 per cent in the number of seniors not paying income tax.

Madam Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to Messrs. Harold Harvey and Richard Beamish, who discovered the disastrous effects of acid rain.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is certainly not with any great deal of pleasure, far from it, that we see the difficulties that many of our companies and many Canadians are facing these days because of the recession.
The hon. member can repeat that every day. He can look at what is happening in the United States, and the same thing is happening in Europe. However, what is happening in Canada that is not happening elsewhere is that our interest rates and our inflation rate are going down. This will create the condition for a renewal of our economic progress.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
In the coming months in the province of Saskatchewan alone, over another 30 farms will have to declare bankruptcy, losing not just their land but also then-dreams, their pride, and a way of life.
Will we have to wait until the entire agricultural sector in western Canada is driven into bankruptcy before the Deputy Prime Minister and the Saskatchewan MPs understand the depth of destruction of their own economic policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern about the situation in Saskatchewan. As I am sure he is aware, the agricultural economy is largely a grains and oilseeds based economy and one that has been affected very seriously by the trade war that has been going on, the result of which has driven prices down to depression levels.
He knows that currently before the House there is a very broad and comprehensive agricultural measure, the Farm Income Protection Act, which speaks to the very point that the hon. member raises.
I appreciate the genuine support that members on our side of the House, and particularly the Liberals, have given toward moving this legislation along. If we can only get some support from the NDP to move it along quickly, we will be able to have it in place for April 1, so that farmers will be able to have the kind of protection which will provide stability and confidence for the future.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Yesterday in Washington Canada's ambassador, Mr. Burney, said that his government would not let the environment get in the way of progress.
By progress, he was referring to the free trade deal which would encourage polluting companies to avoid environmental regulations by moving to Mexico, a country with such lax environmental standards that a 90-second breath of fresh air now costs $2 in the capital city of Mexico City.
March 22, 1991

Would the right hon. minister clarify whether his government shares the view that environmental standards and regulation are an obstacle to progress?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, neither I share that view nor does the Ambassador of Canada to the United States. New Democratic Party members would serve the interests of truth and of their own responsibility if, instead of misquoting Canadians when they declare themselves on important issues, they would quote them correctly.
If you have an issue to join, state the issue honestly. Do not introduce dishonesties into this House of Commons to try to improve your own partisan position.

Madam Speaker, there is one thing you can always be sure of in this Chamber, and that is when you hit a nerve right on with the right hon. minister of external affairs, it is because of accuracy and not because of the dishonesty that he is always trying to flick over at the opposition.
I will quote from the transcript, and this is exactly what Mr. Burney had to say: "What should not happen, in my view, is that environmental concerns should not become the obstacle to progress toward a trade agreement". That is exactly what he said.
Is that the view that Canada is taking into these negotiations, that environment can play second fiddle, that all the polluting industries from Canada can simply move on down to Mexico?
I would like to hear some truth from the minister of external affairs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Why doesn't the hon. member sit down and listen to some truth? He knows very well that what was said by the Ambassador of Canada to the United States was that these two issues have to be pursued with equal speed but on separate tracks. One is not an obstacle to the other.
If the hon. member would adhere to his own earnest demands for the truth, he would tell the truth in this House of Commons and not abuse his place as a member of Parliament by trying to spread falsities across the country.
Oral Questions JAMES BAY AGREEMENT

Yesterday, Mr. Diom Sagamish, Vice-Chief of the Grand Council of the Cree, said:
If we are provoked-and James Bay II is massive provocationthen I will not predict how Cree anger and frustration will manifest
itself. Law and order is not always justice.
Will James Bay be the next Oka? Respect Cree rights and your own
constitution. That is the real answer.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, is the government really prepared to listen? speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should say that the hon. member raises an issue of great concern to all of us. But she should know, and I am sure she does know, that there are leaders of the Cree involved in the discussions about James Bay. Everybody is concerned that there be no further incidents up there.
If the hon. member is as sincere as she always presents herself to be in this House-and as I have said before, I am sure she is-she will work with us to ensure that the concerns of the Cree are addressed in the most appropriate manner and that we work towards a conclusion that will be suitable for everybody.

Madam Speaker, I am really offended and disappointed. I got an invitation from the Deputy Prime Minister to address questions to him on aboriginal issues and he does not answer today. That is appalling.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You want appalling, look in a mirror.

Bravo.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The case of Linda MacDonald is a blight on the Canadian justice system. She was an unwilling victim of brainwashing, funded by the Canadian government in 1963. As a result, she lost her memory. She could not recognize her own children. She had to learn to walk all over again and she even had to be toilet trained.
The Minister of Justice has refused compensation to this person. Will the government reconsider this unfortunate and misguided decision and compensate Mrs. MacDonald?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada

March 22, 1991

the goods and services of the House of Commons to a police officer.

This rate of increase remained well above the 4.8 per cent annual
average experienced in 1990 as price levels continued to reflect the
introduction of the goods and services tax in January 1991.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, why does this government insist on pursuing policies which are so harmful to the Canadian economy and its workers and consumers. Why won't it make some changes to help them right now?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a feeling that this question has been asked and has been answered before.
I will repeat again that Statistics Canada has indicated that inflation rates, the CPI, is coming down. It has come down from early January to now by six-tenths of a point. Interest rates also are coming down and this, I believe, is the result of the only valid policy that can be followed by a government. The former Liberal government did not follow it and Canadians have been paying the price.

Madam Speaker, I would suggest the minister read the Statistics Canada statement which says in part that "the impact of the January 1991 introduction of the goods and services tax can still be felt in prices". Look at the price of clothing-up 9.9 per cent since last February. I ask the minister how such results can possibly help workers and the Canadian economy. Again to the minister; Why is the government so intent on implementing policies such as the GST which have such a devastating impact on our economy?

March 22, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government itself had warned that there would be a one-time increase in the Consumer Price Index, so there is nothing unexpected there. But the government indicated as well that the introduction of the GST would rid Canadian manufacturers and companies of an extremely harmful federal tax and pump $9 billion into the economy, something which would be bound to have a very positive impact.
For their part, Bank of Canada officials also predicted that this temporary adjustment would not have any effect on interest rates and might easily be absorbed by the economy, if you will. That is what is happening now There was a sudden rise at the beginning because the billions of dollars the government had set aside to refund the old tax were not claimed by companies, convinced as they were that the Liberal senators would be successful in their attempt to prevent the adoption of the GST legislation. Such was not the case and, over the past few weeks, we have seen the six tenths of a point decline.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We have learned that as a consequence of the budget recently brought down by the government that the Department of External Affairs is considering cancelling the very important consular facility in Kiev in the Soviet Union, as promised by the Prime Minister during his trip to that country last year.
I would like to ask the minister if he will give us assurances in this House that this very important consular facility, long sought by Canadians of Ukrainian descent and very crucial during these very turbulent times in the Soviet Union will not be a casualty of the government's budget but in fact the plans will go ahead.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if there are casualties, they will not be of the budget but of the long period of excessive spending by Liberal governments that put this country into a situation where it is simply not possible for
us any longer to continue to follow all of the policies we would wish to follow.
A series of budgets have been brought down, which have begun to reverse a trend set in place by Liberal governments, a trend which was deadly to the future of this country. The most recent budget was part of that process. It will impact on all departments. The Department of External Affairs is considering the impact that particular budget will have on some of our activities but no final decision has been taken.

Madam Speaker, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs well knows, the recent Statistics Canada study shows that it is not a problem of spending, it is a problem of monetary policy and that this government has driven up the deficit.
I would ask him again, because we did not get the assurance. He knows that a commitment has been made by the Prime Minister. He knows that this is an extremely important facility at this time in the Soviet Union. In terms of the entire department can we at least ask this specific question? Can the minister assure us that the consular office in Kiev will not be a casualty of the cutbacks now being contemplated in the Department of External Affairs? Can we get that assurance today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Canadians are paying a very high and continuing price for the extravagance of Liberal governments who sat in office as though there would never come a time when we would have to deal with the realities of fiscal responsibility in this country.
This government has recognized, with the broad support of the Canadian public, that those days cannot continue forever. That will have implications for this department as it does for other departments. We are considering the exact nature of those implications. No decisions have been taken on where exactly those limitations may apply.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
As the minister knows, Saskatchewan has been in serious breach of its Canada Assistance Plan agreement with the Government of Canada. The province has denied social assistance, as the minister knows, to
March 22, 1991

entitled people who refuse to participate in work for welfare programs, clearly a violation of CAP. Also, as across the country, welfare rates in Saskatchewan are well below what are needed in order to meet the basic needs of Canadians, another violation of CAP.
After months of promises to look into the evidence in Saskatchewan, will the minister act now to stop Saskatchewan from breaking the law? Why will he not enforce the Canada Assistance Plan agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to refer the House, first of all, to the statements that were made in the hon. member's question. He says I know that Saskatchewan was breaking the law in instituting a work for welfare program.
What I know is that allegations have been made by the hon. member to that effect. What I know is that I undertook to look into the matter, to have it fully investigated. What I know is that the results of that investigation showed that no work for welfare program existed; indeed, we have it in writing from the government of Saskatchewan that they do not have such a policy.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over a year ago, social action groups in Saskatchewan informed the minister, giving him names of people who had been denied social assistance because they had refused to work on the make work programs that the government had provided. He has had information, he has had names, and he has refused to act.
We know the minister does not have a heart, Madam Speaker, but now we know he has no guts. He will not enforce the Canada Assistance Plan.
Why will he not stand up for his responsibilities to poor Canadians? Why does he not take them seriously? Why does he not enforce the Canada Assistance Plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member lacks heart or guts, but he apparently lacks the ability to understand that this government must act on the basis of facts. If the hon. member has facts, none to date which he has tendered, let him bring them forward.

Madam Speaker, what we have done is investigate every allegation that has been made. We have found no evidence which would justify the claims made by the hon. member.
If we are talking about what is lacking, what is lacking most of all here is any substantiation of the claims of the hon. member.

The children's bureau was officially opened this week, six months after its mandate was first announced by the Prime Minister. During those six months, over one million children passed through the lines of food banks. That is more than 3,500 hungry children for each constituency.
How many thousands more will we have to line up before the children's bureau and the Ministry of Health implement the anti-poverty plan of action signed by the Prime Minister at the World Summit for Children?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, along with children's advocates across the country, I welcome the creation of the children's bureau. I was delighted this week to be able to preside over its official opening, although it has been in place for some time.
When the hon. member talks about children's poverty, he should be aware of the fact that since 1984 some 300,000 children in Canada have been able to escape poverty and low income circumstances as a result of the government's policies.
The greatest threat to the future of our children is if we allow our economy to get out of shape and if we allow that massive national debt, that amounts to some $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada, to grow.
It is no surprise, Madam Speaker, when every child being born in Canada inherits a $15,000 debt, that the first thing they do is cry.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.

March 22, 1991
Point of Order
Canada lacks a nation-wide policy on child health. The implications of this for poor children are staggering. They are much more susceptible to injury and death.
Will the minister make it a top priority of the Children's Bureau to develop a comprehensive policy on child health for Canada? Please give a straight answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: A straight answer, Mr. Speaker, that is we are going to do everything we can to improve child health in Canada. We have already taken a number of important steps, including the creation of the Children's Hospital Injury Reporting Program, which is, for the first time, giving us a data base in Canada on children's injuries which will allow us to act in a very proactive way to reduce the deaths and injuries among children. Accidents are the major cause of deaths among children between the ages of 5 and 14 in Canada.

speechtext: I have received notice of a question of privilege.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate that. When we interrupted for Statements by Members and Question Period, I was just reviewing the changes in the tax system and the results of tax reform which are very
positive and have provided concrete evidence of the mistaken assumptions and unwarranted condemnation from the New Democratic Party at the heart of today's motion.
They highlight how the fundamental structural changes we have taken deliver tangible benefits, benefits I might say, assisting Canadians today at a time of economic weakness and hardship, when in fact they are most necessary.
Under our government, Canada's personal income tax system has indeed become more progressive and fair, reducing the burden of taxation on those most in need. The reforms have ensured that those Canadians who enjoy above average incomes are paying the increased share of the national tax burden, which their affluence makes reasonable.
What about corporations? We heard about those this morning. Here again, the opposition's motion is about as outdated as its economics. When we first took office in 1984 we recognized that there were problems with the tax system we inherited when it came to business paying it's share of the national tax burden. That is why in 1987 we introduced measures to eliminate loopholes that had allowed too many businesses to avoid paying any corporate income tax, even when they were fully profitable. That is not all we did.
This motion seems to forget that in order to help in the battle against the large corporations tax, in order to help against the national deficit, the 1989 budget included the large corporations tax. This measure, one of those that opposition members in the Senate, I might say, refused to pass for over a year, ensures that all large corporations will pay tax.
The bottom line impact of these measures is emerging. Government revenue figures for 1989-90 show that at a time of declining corporate profitability, total corporate tax receipts actually increased some 11 per cent. In the banking sector alone, which paid very low levels of tax in the early 1980s, federal corporate income taxes in 1989 amounted to $1 billion, so changes have been made.
In fact, leaving aside the impact of the recession, the over-all impact of tax reform and the large corporations tax has increased the government's revenue from corporate income tax by $2 billion annually compared to what it would be under the previous system. Yes, there are
March 22, 1991

still companies which rate as profitable, but which do not pay corporate income tax, as my friend from Winnipeg Transcona pointed out this morning. However, there is no favouritism involved, no conspiracy against the hardworking taxpayer, no exemption from the struggle to control the deficit.
One of the things he forgets to conveniently mention when he talks about corporations that do not pay taxes in a given year is that he does not go back to see if they had losses in the year before, which of course they can write off. If the profits do not cover those losses, then it is still not a profitable company, although it shows that it made a profit in any given year.
The figures the New Democratic Party stands up in the House day after day and lays on us are somewhat misleading, making it sound like these corporations are cheating the tax system when, in fact, they are not. The combination of tax reform and the large corporation tax should cut in half the number of profitable corporations which do not pay tax. All large corporations will pay tax due to the large corporations tax.
Among the small and medium-sized profitable firms which are not taxed, the majority of these will not pay tax, as I mentioned, because of losses in previous years.
The blunt truth is that this government has taken concrete and historic action to reform the tax system we inherited. By perpetuating the myth of the corporate welfare bum, this motion sadly demonstrates the lack of substance and the absence, I might say, of meaningful alternatives which the combined opposition brings to bear on today's dilemmas. It is political grandstanding at its most cynical best.
There is a related issue I want to address head on which was brought up today by the hon. member. This is the argument that the 80 per cent tax write-off which business can claim on business related meals and entertainment expenses is a tax boondoggle and should be abolished.
This is a claim that blindly ignores the competitive reality confronting Canadian businesses. The ability to deduct these costs as legitimate business expenses is a fact of life in the United States as much as it is in Canada. Both systems recognize that meal meetings and
Supply
business entertaining are legitimate parts of the business process, helping to generate sales, profits and jobs.
My colleague from Pickering has made it very, very clear how, when he was in the business world, a couple of meals ended up helping Canada to the tune of some $60 million in sales.
It is part of the legitimacy of doing business in this country. If Canadian firms were to lose this measure, we would be placing them at a direct disadvantage by increasing the comparative burden of taxation compared to their American companies, i.e., their competitors. It is not a formula for effective debt reduction. Instead, it is a prescription that would ultimately lead to lost sales, lost jobs and finally, lower government revenues. Then we would hear the NDP, up on its feet here in the House, complaining about lost jobs and so on and so forth.
Is this what the opposition wants? I do not think so. Not when it sits down and takes a very close look at this. For the government's part, the fair and proper answer, of course, is no. Absolutely not.
Two days ago at the Debt Freedom Conference, chaired by one of my hon. colleagues, a young Canadian handed the Minister of Finance a cheque for $168. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Transcona made a big deal out of that this morning. This was money which 12 year old Corey Snow had raised through a garage sale and was his contribution directly for the purpose of helping our national debt. At the same conference, other individuals and groups also demonstrated the recognition that the public debt is a national problem which demands a national solution. We are all in it together.
The 1991 budget in its plan for economic recovery is making that solution real and certain. It takes the tough, decisive actions on spending restraint to bring down inflation and to bring down interest rates, so that the deficits for 1990-91 and 1991-92 will be $30.5 billion, despite the difficulties caused by the recession. For 1992-93, the deficit will fall below $25 billion for the first time in a decade; for 1995-96, it will be down to just $6.5 billion.
I want to emphasize, as the Minister of Finance has done with audiences across Canada; there is no misplaced optimism or mathematical mumbo-jumbo at work when we say the deficit will come down to $24 billion by 1992-93.

The fact is that we will no longer be faced with the transitional costs of the GST That represents a $2 billion saving. The gulf war spending will be behind us. The expenditure control plan will deliver incremental savings. Lower interest rates will ease the burden on servicing the debt, and economic recovery will reduce unemployment insurance costs and strengthen government revenues.
In turn, this sharp drop in the deficit combined with national recovery will see the debt begin to shrink as a portion of our economy. This threshold step will mean that government revenues, combined with the continuing benefits of lower interest rates and government spending caps, will be sufficient to eliminate the need for new financial borrowing by the government in 1994-95, a very worth-while goal. That is the target we set out two years ago, in 1989.
In conclusion, in the words of the Minister of Finance delivered to the Debt Freedom Conference here in Ottawa on Wednesday, I am convinced that economic recovery is within our sights. Interest rates have fallen more than four percentage points from the peak last May. Indications are that housing sales are picking up. In fact, The Toronto Star reported earlier this week that the sale of new homes in that city last month was at its highest level in two years.
Following the conclusion of the gulf war, oil prices have returned to near their pre-crisis levels and United States consumer confidence appears to have jumped sharply. Given such stimulus, there is every reason to expect growth to resume by mid-year and to expand by 3.5 per cent in 1992. Just as important, the plan for economic recovery sets us on a path where that growth can be sustained, and confidence and investment flourish in the years to come.
Contributing to that recovery and growth will be the national tax system that we have reformed, based on a concrete and proven commitment to fairness and progressiveness. The facts are evident. It is this motion that fails to meet the test of truth and fairness.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to the motion introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona.
The motion now before the House takes the government to task for implementing a debt reduction program which accepts the savings of children but not those of large, profitable corporations. In other words the responsibility for reducing Canada's debt does not rest equitably on ordinary taxpayers and major corporations. On the strength of the Conservative government's performance since 1984,1 will find it very difficult to believe that debt servicing charges will be shared equitably if ever this debt reduction program becomes reality.
Their reasoning is more for the wealthy and less for the others, more for large corporations and less for small businesses. Such is the doctrine of the Conservatives. No wonder hardship is on the increase in Canada, they create it.
The Tory government has abandoned the traditional role of the government in Canada, which is to redistribute wealth equitably and provide a social security system for the neediest in our society. Since they came to power in 1984, the Tories have been out to destroy all the institutions that provided a safety net for Canadians. They made cuts in the Canada Assistance Plan, they reduced pensions, and now they are going to start on medicare. That is the Tory philosophy: Give to the rich and soak the poor and the average Canadian.
Madam Speaker, I realize we must reduce the debt. However, I don't think the Tory way of doing it is the right way. We should reduce the debt by making everyone pay a fair share. Look at the GST, a consumer tax system implemented by the Tories. Since the GST was introduced and corporate expenses have now become business expenses, corporations can deduct those expenses and claim a credit on the GST paid. For instance, Madam Speaker, the president of a large corporation who goes to a restaurant can claim a credit on the GST paid because he can put the bill on his expense account. This way, a company that claims the GST credit doesn't pay GST. However, a construction worker who buys a sandwich at the mobile cantine pays GST and he doesn't get a credit. That's Tory tax justice!
Let's take a look at what the government proposes. On February 26, in his Budget speech, the Minister of Finance said that any excess funds collected through the GST would go directly towards reducing the debt, after having promised many times that the goods and services tax would be revenue neutral. It was supposed to be a replacement tax to collect money that was formerly collected through the federal sales tax, and it was introduced to replace a system that had become obsolete and was no longer equitable.
March 22, 1991

According to the Budget things have changed, but Canadians have realized for some time that this regressive tax would not be revenue neutral.
Finally, the Minister of Finance realized that the GST would produce a lot of revenue for his government. In his last Budget, he proposed that GST revenues would go directly towards paying off the debt. Clearly, the GST has been selected as the front line weapon to attack our debt. However, the debt we are talking about today doubled in only six years, thanks to the Conservative government. It is a fact that the debt accumulated during the past six years under the Tories equals the amount accumulated between 1867 and 1984, in 117 years. They doubled it in six years. In other words, in six years, the Tory government managed to accumulate the same debt amount that all other governments of this country had accumulated in 117 years!
If it were not for the sinister policies of this government, including high interest rates, the GST would be unnecessary.

Canadians realize that the government's inept economic policies such as the high interest rate policy unnecessarily added to the debt. Canadians are now being asked to pay for the government's mismanagement of the economy with the goods and services tax. Liberals have said all along that this was the largest tax grab in history. But the government said it would be revenue neutral. We were right.
The Liberals said all along that the GST would be inflationary, and again we were right.
We just have to look at the statistics released today. In the month of January we had an increase in the cost of living of more than 2 per cent. The Minister of Finance, when asked, said; this is just temporary, next month it will go away. Well, we had the statistics for February today, and we still have over 6 per cent inflation in Canada. So what happened? What happened there?
Now the government has decided to use the revenue collected from the GST to finance the debt. We must now look at who is paying the GST. I should add, Madam

If the GST is financing the debt, who is financing the revenue collected from this tax? The answer is obvious, and is the essence of the motion in front of us today.
For the record, Madam Speaker, I will tell you who is asked to pay the GST and finance the reduction of the national debt. Students are paying the GST, senior citizens are paying the GST, unemployed Canadians are paying the GST, Canadians on welfare are now paying the GST.

Why does the government want to punish low-income Canadians for the impact of its disastrous economic policies? This government has decided to punish Canadians who are least well off for the present state of the economy in this country. Canadians are not responsible for today's recession. The Liberal Party of Canada agrees with the tenor of the motion before the House today. We believe that responsibility for the debt should be shared equally. This responsibility should never be placed on the shoulders of students, the sick and the unemployed. We believe this policy is deplorable and most unfair.

It is a fact that nearly 40 countries have a GST of sort, but how many have two retail sales tax system? Name one. In most of these 40 countries, there is no sales tax at all. They have what is called a value added tax scheme, a business tax or a goods and services tax, but only Canada has one.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first let me say how pleased I am to rise to discuss this issue today and to say that I, in fact, commend those young children who are concerned about the financial state of the country, are concerned about the deficit and who have been moved to make their savings available to the government. We need to remove some myths about the way the deficit arose. If we do not, we will see this government continuing to put forward its argument, obviously with some success, that its social programs and government expenditures are out of control and must be brought back into line. In other words, those less well-off Canadians, the sick, students, and the young have to pay for the past mistakes of both this government and previous Fiberal governments.

March 22, 1991

A recent secret Statistics Canada study shows that fully 44 per cent of Canada's national debt is due to tax breaks to corporations and to the wealthy. Another 50 per cent is caused by the interest payments and their compounding nature as a result of these revenue shortfalls. Fully 94 per cent of the national debt in Canada has nothing to do with government expenditures or social programs. Indeed, only 6 per cent of the national debt can be attributed to that.
Let's ask how this arose because we are faced with choices. Governments have to and do make choices every day. In this context, the government is making choices which benefit the rich, large corporations and hurt children. Then it is receiving from children gifts to help pay for the deficit.
We do not have to go back very long, but if we go back 15 years, we can see that the Liberals lowered the combined federal-provincial marginal tax rate from 56 per cent to 50 per cent so that richer Canadians pay less tax than they did before.
Once the Tories took office, this process speeded up. First, there was the $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption. There was the lifting of about $6 billion in energy taxes from oil companies.
This government frequently says that we have no alternatives to dealing with the deficit. Let me say that we are concerned about the deficit. There is no point in ignoring the fact that the deficit is a serious problem for Canada, and that we do face with some very tough choices. We do need to reduce it.
We should not be reducing the deficit on the backs of the poor, on the backs of children or on the backs of the sick. We should not be cutting off our opportunity to invest in the future.
A senate committee on poverty recently heard that the financial consequences of Canada's disastrous dropout rate from high school is in the order of $33 billion over 20 years. In other words, if we concentrate our efforts on ensuring that children stay in school, that there was a future for them there and afterwards, this country would save $33 billion over 20 years. It would be an investment in the future. Without making that investment, it is hard to see how Canada will have a future.
We still have over 100,000 profitable corporations paying no tax. We still have thousands of wealthy individuals paying no tax. Over the last years, there has been a reduction in the taxes of the wealthy, and the
figures simply do not substantiate the minister's suggestion that our income tax system has become more progressive. It has not become more progressive.
If we ask the lower income Canadians who have seen their taxes increased, they will tell us it is not more progressive and that it is not fair. They will tell us that they do not want to pay more taxes because the system is not fair.
If this set of government priorities and policies was working, we would be able to see it. After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating, but as a result of these government policies, we have high interest rates, high unemployment rates, record bankruptcies, both corporate and individual.
We have 1.4 million Canadians unemployed and over one million Canadian children living in poverty. Ask them whether this government's policies have worked. They have not worked for those Canadians who are least able to support themselves.
It is time that this government paid attention to those issues. It is not just a question of different political philosophies. It is a question of the future. We cannot continue to ignore the needs of one million children in Canada, fully 20 per cent of our children, and expect Canada to thrive and be competitive in that global economy which is so important to compete in.
The government often says that it has no alternatives. What it really means, of course, is that it has alternatives but it does not like them. We have pointed out those alternatives on many occasions. Basically, one of the alternatives is to pay attention to the tax loopholes that were created by past Liberal and Conservative governments, which gave tax dollars to the wealthy and to corporations, which enabled rich Canadians to become richer, and which enabled business people to entertain their friends for nothing, basically, as a result of the tax system.
Let me just give five suggestions that would save about $5.5 billion. As we have said many times, we could eliminate the $100,000 capital gains exemption. That would save about $1.5 billion. We could eliminate, as has been mentioned, the business and entertainment tax deduction and save another $1 billion. We could eliminate the dividend tax credit and save another $1 billion. This is generally considered to be preventing double taxation of corporate income, but hardly any corporations pay income tax anyway. We could eliminate the
March 22, 1991

manufacturing and processing tax credit, because after all, the manufacturing sales tax is gone. We could remove tax breaks for real estate developers for takeovers and for those multinationals which finance their overseas borrowing at the expense of Canadian taxpayers. Those are just five things the government could do to help reduce the deficit and there is $5 billion right there.
Who would it hurt? It would only hurt the richest of Canadians. This government has chosen not to make the richest Canadians pay their fair share of the burden of dealing with the national debt. It has to be seen as an explicit choice because the evidence is clear. It has chosen to attack the least wealthy, the poorest Canadians.
Over the last few weeks we have seen, as a result of the federal budget, provincial budgets which have severely cut into health care programs, severely cut into the number of hospital beds and the quality of health care available, severely cut into employment in their provinces and severely cut into social assistance programs in those provinces.
The evidence is clear that this government has made a choice and it has made a choice to leave corporations alone and to place the burden unfairly on lower income Canadians.
Coming from the province of Saskatchewan, there is a lesson our governments can give to the federal government. It is not a lesson, of course, that can be provided by the present Progressive Conservative government in Saskatchewan, which started with a balanced budget and now has the highest per capita deficit in the country as a result of its Progressive Conservative ideas.
In 1944 when the first CCF government took power in Canada, Saskatchewan was a bankrupt province and it, I guess, could have decided, had it taken the neo-conservative philosophy of the present Conservative government, to just cut and cut and cut, because after all, it could not afford anything.
In the 20 years that followed, not only did that government move that treasury from one of bankruptcy to one of balanced budgets and surpluses, but it introduced most of the social programs that Canada has come to take for granted. It introduced rural electrification. It
Supply
introduced telephone systems across the province. It introduced medicare, of course.
It is not critical or necessary that a government says: "Because we do not have any money, we cannot invest in the future". In fact, it is absolutely critical that we do invest in the future and that we do not burden the lowest income Canadians, those Canadians who are least capable of fending for themselves.
There is another way. We can cut those tax loopholes to the rich. We can find other sources of revenue. We can stop government waste and we can make sure that we invest in Canadians.
When faced with children coming to the Minister of Finance with their cheques, the minister must have a rather odd view of the world when his economic policies do not work, and when he thinks that taking money from children is an appropriate way to resolve those deficits. Quite clearly this is a manipulation of those children.
Clearly, children will not understand the policies of the government. They are not in a position to judge which politicians are telling the full story. Actually, I am surprised that the minister did not sell these children Conservative Party memberships while he was receiving their cheques. The move to accept the money offered was really I think also a hypocritical one in the sense that the finance minister has been telling Canadians that the deficit cannot be left to our children to pay for, that we cannot leave this burden on our children in the future.
What is he doing now? Instead of leaving for the children in the future, he is taking from the children in the present. What the Minister of Finance should be telling Canadian children is to save their pennies for education and health care because with all of the slashes to social programs, to health care, and to transfer payments to the provinces, those children are going to need that money in the future to buy the services they so critically need.
It is not hard to find other approaches. It is not hard to look across the world and see other economies dealing with these situations in a different way, economies in countries that have governments which put people first as a deliberate political, social and economic choice, and which do not cut social programs and social spending in the hope that some time in the future things will work out.
