What does this government tell those 1 million hungry children who go to school and cannot study because they do not have enough to eat? It tells them: "This is necessary because in the future the country will be better off". That is not the way in which any government should be dealing with its most precious resource, our children and our future. What it should be doing, as I indicated, is investing in them.
I think there are two ways of looking at that investment. Clearly we have to deal with the social, physical and psychological pain that cuts in social programs are imposing on Canadians, but this government does not listen to those arguments requiring compassion. We also can put it in the context of economic terms. As I have mentioned, and as many have mentioned, it simply is not sensible economically to cut into those programs which constitute an investment in our future.
We constantly hear the Prime Minister telling us about the need for a world class education system and at the same time cutting funding to that education system. We can see the consequences across the country. In my own city of Saskatoon, the University of Saskatchewan is now thinking of closing colleges and faculties. What we are doing is cutting off our nose to spite our face. We are cutting off our investment in the future.
While I understand the motives of the children who are seeing the need to pay off the deficit, I think the Minister of Finance needs to look in the mirror in the morning, every morning, carefully and ask himself what he is doing to this country.

Mr. Speaker, I listened patiently to the remarks of my friend in connection with this motion. As he and his party know, we in the Liberal Party are sympathetic to the fact that the government is not sympathetic to the people of Canada.
What I am interested in is the alternatives of the NDP. As I said before, it is easy to criticize. It is another thing to come up with alternatives.
The hon. member said that one of the alternatives he would propose would be to scrap the $100,000 capital gains exemption. I would like to explore that for a moment because, to me, that is a startling proposition. I want him to explain it on behalf of his party so that Canadians can know what we are talking about.
Let us look at the ordinary Canadian. Never mind the fat cats, never mind the people who go to $250 lunches, let us talk about ordinary Canadians who struggle to buy a home, perhaps maybe have a cottage if they are lucky, and maybe have a few investments that they try and accumulate in order to be able to have a secure retirement.
As I understand it, the NDP is proposing that there be no capital gains exemption whatsoever. What does that mean? Does that mean that there is going to be no capital gains exemption for a principal residence? Does it mean that when people sell their principal residence in order to retire into a smaller home, they are going to have to pay capital gain on the value of the increase in the property? Is that fair to the ordinary Canadian? Is that what the NDP is going to propose to the people of this country? Is that what it wants Canadians to understand or is it something else?
No, no, no, it is not on the principal residence, but it is on investments in stocks and bonds. The grandmother who has purchased certain blue chip stocks in order to provide for her retirement and has to cash those stocks in order to buy things will have to pay capital gains tax. A meagre $100,000 capital gains exemption, when, for years and years and years, this country had no capital gains tax encouraging the spirit of enterprise and encouraging Canadians to save and provide for their retirement.
What is it exactly that the NDP is proposing? That there be no opportunity whatsoever for people to better themselves in this country? Is it your policy to scrap the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption, have no capital gains tax exemption? Everybody will be paying more taxes then, never mind the rich.
What is the policy?

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member's comments make a pretty stark contrast between those who want to pursue the interest of the privileged and those who do not. The 1.4 million Canadians who are unemployed, the 1 million Canadian

children who live in poverty are not really persuaded by arguments which help those who are already wealthy to buy summer cottages. Those 1.4 million unemployed Canadians and those 1 million Canadian children living in poverty are not moved by arguments which put summer cottages ahead of food on the table.
If the member would like to listen for just a moment, he will know, and if he has paid attention in the past he will know, that in getting rid of the capital gains exemption we would provide for two exemptions. We would not apply it to farmers and we would not apply it to small business. So, to some extent, the member's screaming and yelling are addressed in those two exemptions.
We understand that there are difficulties that small businesses and farmers face. It is a question of the government making a choice, of political parties making a choice. I will stand up every day for poor children having more to eat as opposed to people being able to buy summer cottages.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member if he could give me a reason why he makes a distinction in his answer. He talked about giving an exemption, in his capital gains formula, to small farmers and small business people and allowing them to have capital gains and, I believe that limit, I do not know if he specified it, could go up to as high as $500,000.
There are many Canadians who do not have that situation of being a small farmer or a small business person. They are people, many of them NDP supporters, who work in companies and earn $30,000, $40,000 or $45,000 a year. They take that money and every year they find they might have $1,000 or $1,500 left over and they want to plan for their retirement.
They buy themselves some stocks in Bell Telephone or some other Canadian company, and as time progresses find that having worked 40 years, having saved a little bit every year, they have managed to accumulate $200,000 or $300,000 they are going to use in their retirement.
If I heard the member correctly, these individuals who have made investments, have made capital gains, are

going to be expected to pay tax on their capital gain, but he exempts the small business person and the farmer.
Would he mind telling me why he picks on senior citizens who happen not to have been farmers or small business people to pay capital gains in this country?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That is easy; the NDP are against seniors.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the argument made is that somebody who has $200,000 or $300,000 saved up should not pay taxes on it. That is the point the member is making.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I would like this member to go to the nearest food bank in his community-after all, there are hundreds of them across this country-and go to the families in that food bank, go to the children and go to the mothers who are trying to put food on the table, and ask this: "Shouldn't we let people with $200,000 or $300,000 get out of paying tax?" That is not just a small number of people in this country, there are 1.4 million unemployed-I don't know how many who are indirectly affected-and a million poor kids.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Enlightening remarks on the part of my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Mr. Speaker, something new for which I commend him.
I think it is important to go over the events since 1984 to respond to the arguments made by my colleague from Saint-Leonard and the NDP members.
The basic principle in this country is that Canadians do not like paying taxes. I know you do not, you told me so. Nobody likes that. But at the same time Canadians have shown a preference for various programs and they want a country where citizens are properly treated. From that point on, taxes have to be paid and collected.
Earlier today my colleague from Saint-Leonard said that in 117 years the national debt had not increased more than the one we now have in 1990 and which, according to him, can be traced back to 1984.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Well put.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
All I can say to him is that the preceding administrations over the 117 years he referred to did not have the unfortunate experience of inheriting a $200 billion debt when they were elected to office. We did, Mr. Speaker. And we are living with it. Since 1984 we have increased public expenditures by only 3 per cent, while provincial legislatures, municipal councils and private sector companies have boosted theirs a lot more than that. We have managed to keep annual increases to 3 per cent, but we did receive much more than that.
In 1984, the federal government was spending $15 billion more annually, on all kinds of programs, than it was collecting revenue. Not 15 million but 15 billion. After six years the federal government is now spending 10 billion less than it collects in revenue. This means a turnover of $25 billion in six years time. That is good management. People will say we raised taxes. Sure, some taxes were raised, but 70 per cent of this $25 billion comes out of cutbacks in the federal government, and only 30 per cent out of tax increases.
And what about these tax increases? Let me explain. Thanks to tax reform, personal income tax for Canadians has gone down. I remember that when I was a tax consultant in Trois-Rivieres, we had 10 tax rates. Not one, not two, but ten, the highest being 34 per cent. After tax reform, we now have three tax rates: 17, 26 and
29	per cent. Before, we had the advantage, and the hon. member for Saint-Leonard who is an accountant will confirm this-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I am listening!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Someone with an income of $100,000 a year had a personal exemption of $3,000, and federal and provincial income tax added up to a tax rate of about 50 per cent. The personal exemption meant that someone with an income of $100,000 was able to save $1,500 a year. However, someone with an income of $10,000 who was paying, let's say 20 per cent income tax, so 20 per cent of $3,000 is $600. The individual with an income of $10,000 saved $600 in taxes and the individual with an income of $100,000 was able to save $1,500, on an annual basis. In 1988 we changed all that and we said there would be one tax credit for everybody. Fair and square: everybody gets the same amount. In fact, this was a tax increase because people with an income of $100,000 who were paying $1,500 less in taxes, are now paying only $1,000 less.
Mr. Speaker, before taxes, if we compare 1984 and today, people are better off. The average salary has gone up from $20,000 to $22,000. The after-tax figure has changed from $18,000 to $19,700, an increase of 8.6 per cent. This means that taxes have gone down as a result of tax reform, no doubt about it.
Tory times!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I hope my hon. colleague has nothing against the 1988 tax cut.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Big deal! After increasing taxes in 1984, 1985, 1986, 1987 and 1988!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1988, the number of Canadians in the $100,000 plus bracket who pay taxes increased by 37 per cent. So, the wealthy individuals not paying their fair, that my colleagues from the New Democratic Party are referring to in their motion, we got them with the tax reform, particularly with the minimum income tax. But we heard no NDPers talk about the minimum tax which, incidentally, was introduced not in 1988 but in 1986. Neither did we hear about the minimum tax imposed on corporations since 1989, Mr. Speaker, or about the cuts in tax shelters: MURBs, limited partnerships, preferred shares, leasing rules. The
30	per cent tax increase I mentioned come from all these
March 22, 1991

cuts in tax shelters, the restructuring of the tax system to make it fair and some taxes which were increased.
My colleague from Saint-Leonard talked about the GST. He said that low-income earners, the students, the underprivileged and the seniors had to pay the GST. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, they do. However, this government did introduce a tax credit. People were phoning me at my office in Trois-Rivieres in December because they were grateful for having received their tax credit cheque before the tax was implemented. The sales tax credit was invented by this government. It is this government, the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of Finance who had this clever idea. So, Mr. Speaker, It is not true that the low-income earners are adversely affected by the GST. They have their tax credit, ahead of time, to be sure. That credit is given to nine millions Canadians who, each year, receive at least one cheque, and the Trois-Rivieres area includes many of them. In fact, that credit is designed to offset the GST, which is a consumption tax, and that mean that if you are rich and you are buying, you pay the tax; if you are not rich and you are not buying, you don't pay the tax. That basic principle was quite relevantly underlined by my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, and is already applied in more than 48 countries. That's no news. France applies the system. It is more complicated than ours and it works.
The 1982 tax reform has cut taxes $2.5 billions. So, Canadians pay $2.5 billions less in taxes since the 1982 tax reform, and that amount is paid by businesses who, as I just said, must pay their fair share. Mr. Speaker, let me quote some figures that speak for themselves. The fiscal reform has made it possible to distribute the tax burden among low and middle income Canadians. In 1987, despite the fact that taxpayers with less than $15,000 income accounted for 47.8 per cent of all filers and 15.3 per cent of all earnings, their share of tax revenues was only 2.1 p. 100 of the total. Compared to 1988, they represented 45.2 per cent of all filers while their share of the tax decreased by about two thirds. In contrast with 1987, taxpayers with $ 100,000 income, representing less than 1 per cent of taxfilers, earned 7.2 per cent of all income but were carrying only 13.7 per cent of the tax burden. In 1988, those same taxfilers earning more than $100,000 have seen their taxes increase by 16.7 per cent. I do not like to give too many figures but I think those
Supply
ones should be mentioned and put on the record to show that this government is efficient and that we have a fair tax system in this country.
True, paying taxes is no fun, but at least the system will be fair from now on. Now, Canadian women and men who earn an income will pay their fair share. And allow me, to answer my colleague from the NDP who says once again that corporations do not pay taxes. This is not true. In Canada, corporations pay their fair share of taxes. He talked about capital gains and I will not come back to that. I think it has already been shown that that argument about capital gains does not hold. He was also talking about the fact that companies are allowed expenses that individuals are not allowed. It is true, Mr. Speaker. It is true that companies are allowed expenses that individuals, that employees are not allowed. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this is normal. Companies must incur certain expenses in the course of their business. So, they are allowed certain expenses, just like unions are.
Mr. Speaker, it is this government once again that cut back on lunches, on automobile expenses. It is this government that said on the issue of meals: there is a part of the meal paid by the company to its employee or to its president that is considered as a personal expense of that individual. That part is no longer tax deductible, but the other part is, because it is a cost of doing business. The individual who pays for his share of the meal, who works for Kruger for example, does is not entitled to any deduction. The owner of Kruger, when he goes to a restaurant with other business people, must pay his own share, it is not tax deductible. This, Mr. Speaker, is an example of fiscal fairness, and I think it disproves what the hon. member for the NDP was saying, that we had done nothing.
He was also talking about dividends. Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of working as a tax lawyer for seven or eight years, and I can tell you that the dividend tax credit is not a gift. It is a tax measure which is part of a whole package. There are two ways for a company to borrow money. It can go to the bank and borrow $100,000 at a rate of 10 per cent and pay an interest of $10,000 a year for it, which is deductible as a business expense. The other way is to go public and to tell the shareholders: "You buy shares for $100,000 and you have a return".

What happens then? After the company pays its taxes, it uses what is left to pay a dividend to its shareholders.
So the company pays dividends to its shareholders from its after-tax earnings. The shareholders are in turn automatically taxed according to their tax rate, but allowance is made for the fact that it is an amount net of tax, that the money has already been taxed when in the hands of the company.
So, the NDP say it is a tax shelter, but that is not true. That money is taxed in one of two ways: either the company chooses to borrow it from a bank or it finds some investors willing to take a chance on its operations.
Mr. Speaker, the NDP is once again talking about the deductibility of interest charges. How could a business possibly function if it cannot take out a loan and deduct the expense incurred on that loan, that is the cost of borrowing money, to improve its machinery, to expand its plant or for some other purpose. It would be unthinkable, in a system like ours, to be unable to deduct the interest charges incurred for operational purposes.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this motion will be defeated, as I am sure it will be. I hope that people on the other side, and particularly the NDP, will stop making comparisons between children-who have a better knowledge of what is going on than the NDP and who are prepared to give whatever little money they have to pay the national debt-and companies or individuals who pay taxes. They are only trying to confuse the Canadian population.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Trois-Rivieres on an excellent contribution to this debate. I would like to make a comment with respect to the motion and to pose a question to him.
This motion was put by the New Democratic Party. It condemns the government for implementing a debt reduction program that fails to ensure that wealthy individuals pay their fair share.
First, it seems to me that it is a little hypocritical of the New Democrats to pose such a motion when the very debt which they speak of is something which they and
their cohorts in the Liberal Party inflicted upon this country during the period 1968 to 1984. Twice they had the opportunity to kill off that unholy coalition. They could have done it in the period 1972 to 1974. They could have done it in 1979, but in each case they crawled back in bed with Pierre Trudeau because he was pushing the same kind of socialist policies that they stand for.
The profligate spending that went on during that time period is what left a legacy of some $206 billion to $207 billion of debt in March 1985, the interest on which, as my hon. colleague pointed out, is something that has severely constrained the ability of the government today to respond to the kind of needs that the country has.
It seems to me that there has been a long list of initiatives taken by this government in terms of getting rid of so-called tax loopholes. The SRTC boondoggle was something that the previous government put forward and cost the Treasury of this country $4 billion or $5 billion dollars. This government curtailed that.
It got rid of the thousand dollar interest exemption, the films, the MURBs, the flow-throughs, and the business investment tax credit. It increased the tax rate on taxable capital gains. As my friend points out, it converted the exemptions to credits. It put on high income surcharges, corporate minimum tax, and so on.
At the same time, every one of these initiatives was opposed by the Official Opposition and by the NDP that posed this motion. At the same every move to refine the tax system and to modernize it was opposed by those opposite.
What I find strangest of all is the inconsistency within the New Democratic Party. This motion calls for the government to tax wealthy individuals, that wealthy individuals should be paying their fair share. A year or two ago, this government put forward measures which would result in the taxing back of the family allowance and the old age pension from high income Canadians.
Guess who opposes that move, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Who?

New Democrats, the very people who want to tax the wealthy and get the rich, really punish them. They
March 22, 1991

oppose the taxing back of the family allowance and the old age pension from these high income Canadians.
Does my hon. colleague not find that approach on the part of the NDP to be completely hypocritical and completely inconsistent?

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments made by my colleague. speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am talking in terms of fiscal policies. The NDP and the Lberals have always been against all of them. It is impossible that they should all be wrong. Nevertheles they are against them. My colleague asked me a question, but there is another one that springs to mind. After looking at the so-called loopholes mentioned by the NDP I explained why they are not loopholes. The next question is that not a day goes by without their asking for more money for this or that. Where do they want us to get the money from? That is the question. So where do we get the money?

It has been six years, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately neither the NDP nor the Liberals have been able to answer that question. They did not suggest practical, intelligent and workable solutions likely to make Canada progress. The role of opposition members is to make the country progress, as is the role of government, and the country will not progress unless they can make suggestions. The have none. They do not make any. Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue on the point that was raised by the previous questioner, that is the question of universality as it applies to family allowances and old age pensions.
Perhaps my hon. friend would agree with me that in effect the policies of the Conservatives have done away with universality as it applies to family allowances and old age pensions. For many years Canadians have been very proud of the net of security that applies to those two programs.
Of course, previously pensions and family allowances did go to families where, regardless of their income, there was in effect a tax back, if we can call it that, as people paid income tax on their total income and these items were included within their total taxable income.
The reason why we have always opposed taxing back the total family allowance is that it denies the principle of caring for the next generation of children. It means that those families who happen to have children are the ones that are penalized.
I do not see why myself and other Canadians who do not happen to have children should not be contributing toward the next generation of children. I am very pleased to do this through the family allowance, which is a universal family allowance, and recognizes the importance of all children. Those who happen to have wealthier parents of course will pay a little bit more on their income tax, but we must really reinstate the whole concept of universality.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand my hon. friend's logic, if there is one. If she feels that all families should get family allowances, I personally feel that only those families who need family allowances

March 22, 1991
Supply
should get them. With all due respect for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney could do without family allowances and still raise his children. Former Prime Minister Trudeau could well survive without his Old Age Security pension. That is the point which my hon. friend does not understand. We feel that family allowances and Old Age Security pensions should be paid only to those who need them. That is the whole point and it does not take anything away from its universal character.
For instance, let us take the case of a senior citizen in my riding who this year is getting a $100,000 income; suppose that next year, for whatever reason, he has no income, he would automatically receive every month his Old Age Security Pension cheque. Universality is maintained for the needy and not for the others. I feel it is simple enough. It is not normal for a person earning $300,000 a year to get family allowances, and later an Old Age Security Pension cheque. It's not normal. He does not need the money, while other Canadians really need it. If we really want the needy to continue to receive the money, we have to take it away from those who can do without it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to speak in this very important debate.
There are a number of items which should be considered in this motion. First of all, the people to our far left are commenting on the fact that the government has stooped to what we did not even think was possible for it, in terms of how low it could go, by publicizing the fact that children are selling their toys to pay down the Minister of Finance's debt.
The second theme involved is, according to the New Democrats, that corporations can do nothing right. Finally, there is the issue of taxation generally.
In my opinion, there is nothing inherently wrong for two or three people in a family to incorporate their family store, hot dog stand, or what have you. One does not have to report that to some great big socialist over there, who rules on the evil of having an incorporated family business.
To that extent, I am going to part company with our friends to the far left. I happen to think that family businesses, small businesses in particular, although incorporated are not necessarily wealthy. The idea that businesses cannot deduct such things as interest on loans in order to buy inventory to sell in their store, according to New Democrat theology, is not something I agree with. I happen to think those kinds of enterprises should be encouraged by all of us in the House of Commons, including those who are socialists.
Let us start with this proposition that we are discussing, namely children.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we will be pleased to speak on supply issues again on Monday. As you know and I think the government has also recognized, there is a lot to talk about in regard to whether or not this Parliament should grant supply to the government. There seems to be that recognition, finally, on the part of the government. We will gladly participate Monday as well as other days, presumably, in order to be able to remind Canadians why this government should be held accountable to an even greater degree than it is right now. We will do our best to do that, until such time as the electors can render the ultimate decision of accountability, which is to turf out the government at the polls the next time.
Let me speak briefly about this issue of fairness in taxation and tax policies generally. First of all, we cannot talk about fairness without talking about the dreaded GST. The dreaded GST is creating tremendous havoc yet. I know the government said it had this science down
March 22, 1991

perfectly and that everything it would do would be correct and good and proper and virtuous. Well, let me read an excerpt from today's Ottawa Citizen which was given to me by my very distinguished and eloquent colleague, the member for Stormont-Dundas.
The member for Stormont-Dundas brought to the attention of the House this morning the issue of crossborder shopping in his area of Cornwall, adjacent to my own constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I quote from the article:
In Cornwall alone, the crossings nearly doubled last month to
77,000 from 43,000 in February 1990.
This government has created taxation policies that are such that people are running across the U.S. border to do their shopping. What do those unfair tax policies do to the businesses of Stormont-Dundas, and of Cornwall, which are so well represented by my colleague? What did they do?
What did he do to the good people of Glengarry- Prescott-Russell and other Canadians who own businesses in this country? Now, of course, we have our good old socialist friends governing Ontario. The good old socialists of Ontario, the friends of Peter Kormos, remind me a little bit of a dog that caught the wheel of a car as it was going by. They are asking now: what do we do with it?
The members of the NDP in Ontario protested Sunday shopping. They protested Sunday shopping so loudly and with such virtue and wholesomeness and all that good stuff that the NDP does so well, thinking of course that they would never have to deal with the issue because the courts had decided on it. Lo and behold, a couple of days ago the Supreme Court of Ontario ruled that in fact the government of Ontario-the NDP government now, of course; need we be reminded-had the authority to rule on Sunday shopping.
It was easy to be against Sunday shopping when they knew they would not have to rule on it. But now they are going to have to rule on it and the law that had been disbanded is all of a sudden back in place. At the same time, communities along the Canada-U.S. border on the Canadian side are being affected by this Sunday shopping issue. We are anxiously waiting to see how the friends of
Supply
Peter Kormos handle this particular question. We shall wait anxiously for probably a few more somersaults, handstands and headstands on the part of silk stocking Bob and his good comrades at Queen's Park. We shall wait and see how to deal with that.
Let us come back to the issue of fair taxation, the GST and other matters. We have the whole issue of fair taxation by the government across the way to contend with. That is no small potatoes.
I have a letter from a constituent of the great riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell that I am going to read to you. Some of the issues he brings to our attention concern the unfairness of the taxation system of the government across the way.
He says in his letter: "If I am at work or home, and I am unfortunate enough to become involved in an accident or suffer a heart attack or other illness which might result in my death, the proceeds of my life insurance policy are not taxable income." Fair and good and proper, in so far as I am concerned. However, let us continue: "If I am at work and become involved in an accident that leaves me disabled for a period of time, and I receive Worker's Compensation benefits, these are not subject to income tax either." Again, that is reasonable.
However, listen to this: "If I am at work or any other place and I am unfortunate enough to suffer a stroke or a heart attack which leaves me disabled but still alive, and I receive disability insurance, it is considered to be taxable and are subject to income tax."
Anyone who thinks that kind of policy is reasonable and fair, has their head screwed on wrong, in my opinion. I wrote to the Minister of Finance about this issue last September. He has not even responded yet. He has not even responded to this very legitimate grievance on the part of a constituent who is trying to obtain redress. I know: "The answer is in the mail."
I have another constituent who corresponded with me recently about another issue involving unfair taxation. I am glad to see that the President of the Treasury Board is here, because perhaps he can note these questions I am asking. I see he is getting out his notebook, he wants to note this. Perhaps he can take note of this question and forwarded it to his boss, the Minister of Finance.

I wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance about an issue that was brought to my attention by another constituent in regard to child custody issues.
As members know, there is such a tax rebate device as the child tax credit. The child tax credit is another very reasonable proposition. It is given pursuant to whichever parent has custody of the child on the last day of the year. I have constituents who are unfortunate enough to have parted company, in other words they are divorced. The child lived with one parent for 11.5 months of the year and then, pursuant to mutual arrangement, moved in with the other parent. Guess which parent gets the child tax credit? The one who kept the child two weeks, not the one who kept the child 11.5 months.
I wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance on this issue. Do you know what his answer was? He said that it would be too complicated to calculate this kind of thing and that is why he does not intend to change it. This is Tory fairness. This is the explanation I get from the Minister of Finance.
I cannot believe that the Minister of Finance, who claims that he can count all the money we need to run the government in Canada, cannot count the child tax credit for my constituent. Perhaps this explains the reason why we are in this much trouble in this country; the Minister of Finance cannot count.
Over the last couple of weeks, I have been receiving phone calls from automobile dealers in Glengarry- Prescott-Russell concerning the GST refund to automobile dealers. Twenty-one days.

Twenty-one days. Well, what is the difference? It has been close to three months and they have not received one cent. I have not yet found one car dealer who has managed to get the money back. This is Tory fairness. I have to admit it, they are making more businesses in the constituency that I represent go bankrupt because they are hanging on to funds that do not belong to the government; those funds belong to my constituents to operate their businesses and to make them survive.

The rate of unemployment in my riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is 16.6 per cent. Why would we want such unfair policies that cause more pain, suffering and hardshihp to the people of Glengarry-Prescott- Russell?
A moment ago, Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity to discuss with my colleague from Newfoundland, the member for the riding of-

The parliamentary secretary said in this House that since 1988, taxes were fairer or something like that. I am paraphrasing here. The Conservative members across the way are talking about this fairness in taxation policy. Let me tell you what is happening here. A family of four making between $25,000 and $30,000 a year, hardly a rich family- they would not even be considered rich in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell-

I want to talk a little bit about the issue of the Minister of Finance standing in front of the television cameras with children who had sold their toys in order to pay part of the deficit. I have not yet seen anyone sell a limousine

to help pay part off the deficit. Speaking of limousines, I meant the used car lot that is outside the west door of the Parliament Buildings when we leave after a vote at night, namely the ministers' limousines.
Speaking of that, if this government were serious about restraints why are there 40 cabinet ministers to handle the affairs of this nation? In the United States, a country 10 times the size, there are fewer than half the cabinet ministers. With 10 times the population, if they can do the job of running the country with half as many people, and I recognize that Tories are only half as efficient as most of the rest of us, but do you not think they could at least do a little better than they are doing now? Could the government at least show an example? Speaking of selling toys, maybe it could sell some of those big toys, those great big dark-blue toys outside the west door here, chauffeur driven and all.
I say to the government across the way that it needs to preach restraint far better by practising some of it itself. I say to the government that it needs to establish fair taxation policies for families and for everyone else. Numerous letters I have received over the last 12 months are from couples with children who are telling me they are financially disadvantaged because they are married. I have complained many times to the Minister of Finance about that. In regard to taxation there is such a thing as the spousal equivalent exemption, or something like that. What effectively that does is it allows an adult to place a child as a deduction, the same as if it were a spouse, which effectively means that married people cannot do something that two people unmarried and living together can do. In other words, each one of them can claim a different person as being the spousal equivalent.
I do not think there should be policies in this country which discriminate against families. If they are not advantageous to families, well I still do not like it, but at least it is fair game. At the very least, one would think that one should not be worse off for being married in this country and raising a family and so I ask the government for some fairness in that regard.

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member who just spoke on debate. What I like about the hon. member's contribution to this House is that he always has his ear to the grass roots in the riding and across

Canada. He knows the impact of policies created in this House on the average person out there in our ridings.
He talked about the bankruptcies reported in most newspapers yesterday and in The Financial Post, John Geddes writes under the heading "Bankruptcies continue to soar":
Ontario and Newfoundland were hit hardest in February as the recession drove 6,249 businesses and consumers across Canada into bankruptcy, up 68 per cent from a year earlier.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question from my colleague. The bankruptcies have affected the constituency that I represent very severely. It is not just bankruptcies. There are partial and otherwise plant lay-offs as well. For instance, the Ivaco steel mill in L'Orignal, Ontario laid off a number of workers a few weeks ago. Canadian Pacific Forest Product Research Lab in Hawkesbuiy, a lab which had been there for 80-odd years, formerly known as CIP Research, is now shutting its doors; 62 people in very good jobs, a lot of them scientists and so, on all losing their work.
There have been many lay-offs at textile plants in my riding as well. Plants have been shutting down, plants have been in some cases going out of business. In some places there are just partial lay-offs. A year ago we lost one industry in Hawkesbuiy, a garment factory known as Canadelle. It manufactures under licence from a company known as Wonder Bra. Some 100 people lost their jobs, as far as I know, all women.
The announcement was in October 1989. The plant closed February 2, 1990. Officials from the Government of Canada met with the people immediately. The local Canadian Employment Centre was there I think the night that they announced the closure or the day after and I was there with it.
To this day, the Program for Older Workers' Assistance-I think it is abbreviated to POWA-for older workers who are losing their jobs; these women who are, many of them, well into their fifties, as of today, March 22, 1991 still do not have an answer as to whether or not they will qualify for the program for older workers assistance. Some 16 months after it was announced the factory was to shut down, 14 months after it did shut down, and I was told yesterday that it would take at least two more months before they will be told whether or not they will get their money.
There is 16.6 per cent unemployment. Grandmothers are not the first people who are going to be rehired, anyway. When there is 16.6 per cent unemployment it makes it that much worse. And that is why there is a program for older workers assistance, which I believe was initiated by the previous Liberal government.
But it is taking so long, 15 or 16 months, to get then-money, and to make matters even worse-and I think I am really getting to the centre of the issue raised by my colleague-at the same time as they are having to wait for this, their unemployment insurance benefits have been cut back. Previously they could draw unemployment for a year, so if it took a year to qualify for the program for older workers adjustment, they at least had something else in the meantime. But now they have run out of UIC and are presumably on welfare, or whatever, until they qualify for this assistance.
I could not get an answer from the government as to why someone had goofed and allowed all this time to go by and not provide a positive answer for the employees of Canadelle in Hawkesbury.
This morning I wrote a letter to the Minister of Labour asking for his intervention, personally, and of course I will not have an answer for a little while, but I plead with him to assist those women who were working at Canadelle so that they can get some benefits instead of going on welfare.

I would like to make a comment and put a question to my hon. colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
I think it is a bit ironic that we on this side have to listen to lectures from the Liberal Party on how to manage the economy and how to reduce debt, given that
March 22, 1991

it is the party which, between 1968 and 1984, over-spent. It has no regard whatever for spending limits. This government in its recent budget has proposed to legislate, for the first time in history, spending limits.
The only regret I have is that it was not done a long time ago. Indeed, had those spending limits been in place back in the late sixties, we would not have the problem and we would not have the need for the motion today.
It was easy back there during the seventies. It was the credit card operation-the Liberals didn't have the guts to face people with the cost of the programs. It was just a matter of shovelling out the vote-getting programs and not worrying about it, we will let the next generation pick up the bills.
Unfortunately, it has come back now, and you can tell that they can't stand to hear it because they know very well that it is the truth.
Take sales tax reform, for example. As far back as 1940 a royal commission suggested that there be sales tax reform. Commissions after that made numerous suggestions, but never, never in all the years that the Liberal Party was in power did it have the backbone to take that initiative.
For example, they oppose in this House any and all measures to reduce expenditures, to curtail programs that are not necessary, oppose every effort to increase revenues.

That is a bit like being in favour of virtue. Everyone is in favour of virtue. I am just not in favour of driving the people in my riding out of business. That is the problem I have with what this government has done.
The great redeemer across the way has asked me to provide a constructive idea of how to cut expenditures. Well, I am glad he asked. I was a little curious, so I put in an access to information request to see how much bottled mountain stream water was being purchased for the office of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate today.
It used to be a common joke that would be told at neighbourhood gatherings when the parents would get together after the kids had gone to bed and share with each other some of the disconcerting things that their children had done to them that day, memorable events such as using a vacuum cleaner to extract a toothbrush

March 22, 1991
Supply
from the toilet or exhibiting artistic talent with magic markers all over the wall. Some parents would comment: "The best revenge is to live long enough to be a problem to our children".
That is no joke today. We even see bumper stickers with such sayings as: "I'm out spending my kids' inheritance" or "I'm going to live long enough to be a problem to my kids".
That is really a problem for our children, and the revenge we are placing on them is far from sweet. It is very sad and it is very sobering. Our revenge is the national debt, a debt that if we leave unaddressed will be a painful inheritance forced on our children and their children and their children.
Many of us were children in the 20 to 25 years from 1950 to 1973. Madam Speaker, I know that would include you; it certainly includes everybody on this side of the House. We grew up during a period of record economic growth and personal prosperity, and we saw a standard of living virtually double in a single generation in that period of time when we were children. Inflation was less than 3 per cent, interest rates were low, and the federal deficits were small or non-existent. We ran a plus or minus on an annual basis, and the economy was functioning well.
As a result, we grew up with confidence that prosperity and economic growth were normal things. It was almost inevitable that we would have prosperity. Our ability to meet and solve the problems and challenges of these years was only constrained by our creativity to define the solutions and a determination to see them through to their conclusion.
But then from 1974 through to 1984, and I might add even a few years subsequent to that, the way was lost. In these 10 years or so inflation soared. We tried to buy our way out of each and every new problem.
The result was very predictable. The federal deficit jumped at one point to $38 billion and the national debt grew from some $27 billion in 1974 to over $200 billion in 1984 and now to almost $380 billion.
Here we are thinking about the closing years of our careers and watching with concern, even trepidation, as our children are just beginning to assume their roles as adults in the society we are destined to leave them.
It is not simply the size of the debt that ought to concern us. It is the very tiny margin of financial flexibility that we are in fact leaving to our children. They like every generation will have their own challenges to meet, some of them about which we do not even know today as to what possible challenges they might have. At the very least we owe our children the opportunity to invest in the benefits of the prosperity they create and the solutions they apply to the challenges of their time.
Instead, we are on the verge of constraining their creativity and their capacity to meet the future by forcing them to pay for the past. This is not the future this government, this party or I would intend to leave to my children and the children of Canada.
Since the first budget and the first thrown speech back in 1984, our government has been committed to two important principles. The first is to maintain a level of social programs that enables all Canadians, young and old, to participate fully in Canadian society. In some areas of high priority, the government does not hesitate to expand its commitment.
The second is to plan year by year the control of our deficit so that our children's future options will be available to them and will not be curtailed by the need to clear away a legacy of financial irresponsibility.
The Canada Assistance Plan, which has certainly received an awful lot of attention in the last few weeks in the press, in spite of misleading assertions to the contrary remains a major component of Canada's safety net. Over $5.2 billion will have been transferred to the provinces in matching money this year to help finance social assistance payments to individuals in need and social programs of support. This will increase by some 7.3 per cent to over $5.6 billion in this coming year.
True, increases to the three wealthiest provinces, the province of which I am a resident and in which my constituency is located, are capped at 5 per cent; but the open-ended arrangement for the other provinces certainly remains intact.
In excess of $550 million of the CAP expenditures are in fact applied to child welfare services for an estimated 50,000 children in care and another 250,000 served annually through various child welfare protection services provided in their own home or in the community surrounding. These services include information and
March 22, 1991

referral services, clinical counselling and also homemaker services.
The Family Allowance Program provides a taxable benefit to over 6.6 million children in 3.7 million families. This fiscal year over $2.6 billion will pass through this program to families with children.
The child tax credit, a more targeted benefit program for low and middle income families, represents another $2.2 billion of income supplementation in next year's budget.
I remind hon. members that the government has doubled the maximum value of this program since 1984, in recognition of the importance it plays to low income families with children. A special supplement for low income families with young children under the age of seven has been added to the benefit package.
Despite the deficit, however, the government's commitment to maintaining a sound safety net remains and, in areas of particular priority, it has been enhanced.
There are other important initiatives that represent the government's determination to confront new problems as they come up. In a direct response to the landmark research report on sexual abuse of children by Dr. Badgley and his committee, sponsored by the federal government, a major initiative was begun in 1986. Sexual abuse of children is a horrifying reality of life for some children for many years. I am sure every member in this House would agree that is a terrible situation. It was scarcely mentioned prior to the late 1970s. That is no one's fault; it was just not mentioned. The problem has always existed, as Dr. Badgley's report proved beyond any doubt, but it was simply hidden away beneath fear, disbelief and denial.
Between 1986 and 1990, the federal government committed $25 million to begin addressing this hidden horror. In 1988 the government introduced an additional $40 million over four years to extend the reach to address violence in the family.
The success of these initiatives and the exceptional efforts of provinces, professionals, individuals, including children and adults who came forward to deal openly with their pain, has not been easy for Canadian society to absorb.

The federal government brought forward major improvements in the Criminal Code and Canada Evidence Act to better protect children and ensure that they might be heard in the courts of our land.
Important advances in treatment and prevention were supported through this initiative. A special adviser to the Minister of National Health and Welfare was appointed with a mandate to recommend the next phase of federal action.
Last month, in response to Mr. Rogers' report, the Minister of National Health and Welfare introduced a much enhanced $136 million four-year program to continue the effort of reducing the levels of family violence in Canada.
Over 90 per cent of the special adviser's recommendations in areas of federal jurisdiction will be acted upon in whole or in part over the next four years.
The new family violence initiative will assist with training of judges, physicians, nurses and social workers, whose knowledge and experience are critical in dealing effectively with both victims and offenders.
Treatment to offenders will be provided in all 60 federal correctional institutions.
In consultation with aboriginal communities, 2,000 health care and social workers serving Indian reserves and Inuit communities will be trained, and prevention programs for over 500 communities will be developed with the assistance of aboriginal leaders.
Productive partnership will be forged with community organizations, service groups, unions and business.
This program is more than twice the size of the government's previous effort and stands as confirmation that the federal government has not lost its will to confront and address major social issues of our time.
But let us be clear about the nature and the scope of the issue that lies before us. In the report's opening remarks, Mr. Rogers, the special adviser writes:
My life has been deeply marked by my experiences of the last two years as Special Adviser to the Minister of National Health and Welfare on the issue of sexual abuse. I have been shocked by the anguish and pain of so many victims and adult survivors. I have also come to understand that this problem is so pervasive that any child could be a victim of sexual abuse, including my own children and grandchildren.

He says in his concluding remarks:
The changes we need to make in Canada, both at a prevention and
public education level, as well in co-ordinated services to those in
need, require the concerted and inclusive support of all.
Because the needs of Canadian families are changing, especially due to the increased number of women entering the work force, the government has made important changes in parental benefits. Fifteen weeks of maternity benefits are now available during the period surrounding the birth of a child. Ten additional weeks of parental benefits are now available to natural or adoptive parents. Fathers or mothers can take these benefits or share them between themselves.
Of considerable importance to many working parents is the provision of child care services. Canadians have expressed their wishes to have considerable choice in the child care that they seek for their children.
Through the Canada Assistance Plan, for example, the government is providing a quarter of a billion dollars in support for child care for low income Canadian parents and a further $600 million plus through tax provisions, the child care initiative fund and dependent care allowances for persons on training courses.
We are increasingly aware that marriage breakdown is often the cause of a slide into economic difficulty, even poverty for the spouse that maintains the responsibility for looking after the children. Departing spouses, unfortunately most often fathers, too readily forgo their ongoing financial support of their children. To respond, the government through its Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act is providing for the release of information which can assist in locating those defaulting spouses and the garnishment of pensions, income tax refunds or other federal payments.
There are many specific programs for children and families that are developed by the federal government, usually in consultation or partnership with many fine national or community based voluntary organizations with well-known expertise in issues and services affecting children.
Specifically I would like to reference three that have been successful. These programs were created to provide
practical information and guidance to parents about their child's development and their own changing responsibilities to the children. The Post-Partum Parent Support Program is a resource for new mothers. Nobody is Perfect is a program that emphasizes the parenting skills for parents of children up to five years, and Ready or Not is a resource for parents of children eight to twelve years old.
One final recent initiative by the government is also worthy of mention. It is called CHIRPP, which stands for the Children's Hospital Research Injury and Prevention Program. Its creation was the result of two very basic facts. First, injury is the number one killer of Canadian children, accounting for approximately half of the 5,500 childhood deaths to children under the age of 19. Second, while we knew the number of injuries and the type of injuries, we do not know much about the specific causes of these injuries. CHIRPP is helping to study the causes by monitoring each childhood injury upon entry into a number of selected hospitals.
Detailed interviews are taken from adults and children if possible at the reception desk which seek to determine just how that particular injury occurred, the circumstances and the environment which caused it. The results are computerized within the Department of Health and Welfare. In the near future we hope to have a full analysis and an understanding of the causes as they are indicated.
Perhaps one of the most significant recent events that has occurred with great long-term potential for children in Canada and throughout the word was the September 1990 world summit for children held in New York. Leaders of 70 nations gathered to discuss and adopt a declaration on the survival, protection and development of children.
Canada was one of the six countries that initiated the summit and our Prime Minister was asked by his colleagues to co-chair its proceedings. It was a unique event and certainly a very significant success. The summit was not meant to be the end of interest in children but the catalyst that demonstrates the potential good that can come from attention focused on children.
March 22, 1991

The potential is real enough. The declaration goes on. It contains a 10-point program which all nations are urged to work toward implementing over the coming decade.
Canada was a major participant in the development of the convention through a federal, provincial and territorial working group. Through the continued effort to complete the required legislative review by the federal, provincial and territorial governments, it is anticipated that Canada will ratify the convention in 1991.
I began by talking about the crushing financial burden we could leave to our children if we do not address the implications of a growing deficit and debt. I am reminded that last year the money Canadians spent on the interest payments to service our national debt exceeded the expenditures on all programs administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. This includes the national health care programs, the welfare programs, the Old Age Security and family allowance support programs.
Imagine the potential of this amount of money in implementing the 10-point program of the summit's declaration not only here in Canada but for children throughout the world. UNICEF projects that $20 billion of new money per year is needed to achieve the minimum conditions for children in developing countries outlined in that 10-point program. Of that, $7 billion will be needed in the form of international aid from donor countries.
It is a considerable sum, but not as great as our annual deficit. We must seize the problem of our deficit. We must maintain our levels of social investment. It is not easy, and the answers are not simple. But we have begun on the difficult path to improve our legacy to our children. May they at least credit us, finally, with having recognized the problem and carefully planned our way toward its resolution.

Madam Speaker, in his opening remarks the hon. member paid compliments to his party. He said that it had two main goals. One was in its social policy, to maintain a certain level of social programs. The second was in its economic policy, to plan year by year to control our deficit. Again
Supply
we hear this crying the blues, blaming the Liberals for piling up the public debt.
When the member's party came into office the public debt was $177 billion and now it is running up to $400 billion. I was here from 1979 to 1984. He can blame the Liberals for increasing the public debt up to $177 billion at a time when we were going through world recessions, not Canada-made recessions.
What did his government do with all the money that it collected for selling off Crown corporations? Why didn't that go to reducing the annual deficit further and reducing the public debt? What did his government do with the 33 tax increases that it brought in, in the seven years it has been in power? To that end, the coalition will soon launch a "mass action" campaign -including petitions, advertising and demonstrations -to protest what it says are the de-Canadianizing policies of the government.
Mr. Clarke goes on to say:
"We believe we have to move quickly or the country will be so changed by the"-

speechtext:

The hon. member may want to put a question to the hon. member for Ontario who has completed his speech, but I really cannot agree with these types of comments.

On a point of order, Madam Speaker, I did begin by pointing out the social and economic policies the member mentioned in his speech. My closing comment is quoting Mr. Clarke where he says:
"We believe we have to move quickly or the country will be so changed by the government's economic and social policies that we won't be able to save it,"

March 22, 1991
Supply
I would like to hear from the member that if he was out to save the economic and social policies of this country, why this massive campaign to defeat his government?

Madam Speaker, I certainly would like to respond to that. The hon. member started off on a comment that I laid the blame on the 10 years from 1974 to 1984. I also believe that in my comment I said that it carried on through 1989 and 1990 when the debt in fact went up to some $380 billion.
I do not absolve the federal government of the last five years of the financial problem that this country has. I would point out that between 1974 and 1984 the debt of this country increased some eightfold. It only doubled in the time we were here. In either case it is a terrible number, but the fact of the matter is that we are trying to address it.
Further, I would like to respond to the hon. member's comment about all these tax changes. I note that in the election campaigns and in many other opportunities which the Liberals take advantage of they complain about the 33 tax changes and how terrible they are. Of course what we were addressing were loopholes that they had put in place. They consider it terrible that we issued a measure to prevent a variety of schemes of transfer tax losses from non-profitable corporations to profitable ones.
The Liberal Party disagrees with the reduction of a variety of special purpose investment tax credits. It disagrees with an increase in the rate of taxation on capital gains. It disagrees with the introduction of a corporate surtax. It disagrees with the introduction of put-in-use rules to limit the use of deductions where taxable income is not forthcoming. It disagrees with the removal of the inventory allowance. It disagrees with the curtailment of the use of leasing to transfer benefits for accelerated capital consumption allowances, and disagrees with a credible tax on large deposit-taking institutions, most recently the large corporation tax which has been adopted to ensure that all large companies contribute to deficit reduction. The Liberals disagree with literally all of these good steps and then complain about the fact that the government is not spending enough money.
The whole issue of the debate today and the budget we brought down is deficit and debt. We are not about to ignore these problems in our role as government.

Madam Speaker, the previous speaker began his remarks by talking about the parties that parents attended without their children to talk about the cute familial antics of their children during the day or during the week. That may very well be.
Obviously the member has not been to one of these parties lately because I have news for him. When the parents get together today without their children to talk about things, what they are doing is asking themselves how in heaven's name they can rid themselves of a government that they thought was going to do something for them when it came to power in 1984 in a landslide election victory.
They talk about the fact that when they take little Billy, or little Susan, to have his or her hair cut they now have to pay tax on that hair cut. When they want to go to a children's store to buy a children's book they have to pay tax. When they want to take that child to one of the few movies that a parent can take a child to today, without worrying about obscene language or anything else, they have to pay tax on that. That does not affect the rich. That affects the poor. That affects the lower income Canadian. That is what those people are talking about today.
The member went on to talk about the terrible deficit, and indeed it is terrible, and to his credit he admitted, and I believe his words were that it went on some years beyond 1984, as indeed it has. He suggested that his government is attempting to deal with it.
What Canadians are asking at these little parties he referred to is how the government is attempting to deal with it. We have had his finance minister for seven years and one economic statement make predictions that time and time again have been completely wrong. Throughout this time they are not tax changes but tax increases that we are talking about.
Lower income Canadians are paying more tax today than they did in 1984 and higher income Canadians are paying less tax than they did in 1984. Those are the facts. What is this government doing to tiy and help those people with children who are struggling in today's society, trying to reduce a deficit that is $30 billion after six years of alleged tough times under the Tories when we have had a strong economy? What in heaven's name,
March 22, 1991

they ask at these parties the member referred to, is going on and how can we get rid of this government?
I ask the member how much tax is too much tax? How many times are you going to tax the Canadian people in an attempt to pay down the deficit when after six and a half years all you have done is double it?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the member's question. His riding is very close to mine and I presume economically we confront very similar bases and issues.
I can tell you what happens in my riding at those parties I attend which are obviously different than the parties he attends in his riding. In my riding they do talk about the fact that they have to pay tax on books that they never had to pay before. They have to pay sales tax on the magazines. They have to pay sales tax on the clothing, and they have to pay sales tax on some things, hair cuts, that they never had to before.
They talk about that in my riding, and I am sure they talk about it in his riding, however, in my riding what they also say is: "You know, this is a fair tax, because everybody pays." We in our riding, much like his riding where there are many high income Canadians, also say: "Thank goodness that the government saw the light to put in place a sales tax credit for those low income Canadians who are impacted by the GST".
In my riding the people say that is a fair tax. In his riding, unfortunately, I guess they forget about mentioning that low income credit, and that is probably because in his riding nobody receives that kind of credit because it is a very well-to-do riding.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for a few minutes on this motion because it does give me an opportunity to talk about some of the issues which have been brought up in the debate in the last hour or two.
The motion states very specifically that rather than try and unload the deficit by having children subsidize part of it, that we should do it, as the motion says, through programs which accept the savings of children but fail to ensure that large profitable Canadian corporations and wealthy individuals pay their fair share.

March 22, 1991
Supply
Today we have had a number of members state that we in the New Democratic Party do not recognize who is wealthy and who is not wealthy. It is very interesting to note that if a survey was taken of the people of Canada who are members of the three political parties, it would show that the highest earning group in Canada are the New Democrats. We are always told that we represent the poorer people of the country, and we do, but we do that out of principle. We have become over the last few years the highest earners as far as the membership in the three parties is concerned.
I guess it proves that the people of intelligence who take a look at the issues, take responsibility for what is Canada and what makes Canada work, support the kinds of policies that we in the New Democratic Party have espoused over the years.
More than espousing, we have made them part of the fabric of Canada. Consequently, people say: "Yes. Regardless of how it affects us taxation-wise, we are quite willing to support that kind of policy."
We also know that over the past few years, because of the structure of the atmosphere under which businesses and farmers have had to work to take advantage of the protection that has been placed through corporations, a lot of us have decided it is worth while to accept the corporate structure.
It does protect us from the government and from other corporations. Consequently, we do so. Most of those corporations, which we do not consider wealthy as defined in this motion, are owned and operated by the same people. That kind of corporation is not much different than a small business that is not incorporated.
Consequently, it is not going to be affected by major taxation differences in the same sense that we are talking about in this particular motion.
We have indicated many times across the country that we think one of the changes should be on capital gains. In our policy, we eliminate certain groups from having to pay capital gains.
The aim of our policy is not to take the capital gains of that farmer who has spent his life building up a farm that
he thinks will be worth while when he finally does retire and can use the gain to keep him in retirement.
The same kind of approach has to be recognized in small business, which is quite often a family operation. Everybody's time and effort is put into the building of that business. Farmers probably do not have retirement plans, although they need them. We have exempted those people from capital gains.
We are aiming at those unearned capital gains which are part of speculations within share sales. The purchasing and selling of homes other than one's principal home or cottage at high prices are unearned capital gains. They are speculative gains.
There is not a great deal of sweat or effort. When we say that capital gains should be taxed in some way, we are talking about the kinds of capital gains which are almost unearned. They are speculative gains.
Farmers and small businesses, also, do not have the protection that wage earners have. One of the questions by one of the members in opposition was: What about the wage earner who does gather a lot of money, makes an investment and then can sell it at a higher price?
Most of those people are quite willing to pay capital gains on what they gain in that speculative process. During the period in which they were earning the money to put a payment down on that cottage, extra home or extra investment, they were protected by unemployment insurance which no farmer or small business has.
If one owns a business or farm, one does not have unemployment insurance to fall back on in those days when one does not get a crop or when business is really bad.
There seems to be a very bad recognition of what is meant by regressive and progressive taxation.
Progressive taxation means that if you earn enough money to have a good living and something extra besides, you should be taxed a little more on that extra than the person who just earns enough to survive. Any suggestion that the same amount of taxation should be paid across the board is a regressive sort of approach. Progressive taxation, in contrast is tax which takes an increasing percentage of the earnings of an individual.
March 22, 1991

The GST is a regressive tax, because if you spend $1,000 on goods and services, you are going to pay 7 per cent on that $1,000. That means you are paying 7 per cent of your earnings to the GST However, if you earn three or four times that much and you only spend half of it on goods and services, you are going to be taxed only 3-1/2 per cent on your total earnings. In other words, the person earning more is paying a smaller percentage than the person earning less.
That is regressive taxation. That is what we have been working against.
There have been suggestions made a couple of times today that because we are against the taxing of family allowance and the taxing of old age security, we are flip-flopping in the sense that they say that is tax against the rich and that we should agree with it because we are always saying that we should tax the rich.
We have to recognize that the thresholds established both in the case of the family allowance and the old age security taxes are such that now, and certainly within a few years, will be so low that a person earning a moderate income is going to have to pay more. In each of these cases we have to look at the unfairness. If one person earns $10,000 and part of it comes from the old age security or family allowance, and another person earns $10,000 and none of it comes from those, the first person will pay more taxes. It is unfair.
Supply
If the taxable portion of the salary of a person who is getting the senior citizen's allowance or the family allowance is the same as a person who is not, the former will be taxed more than the latter.
I could go on and tell of a number of things that we as New Democrats think should be put in place.
In the last budget the government had a number of choices. For instance, it could have increased the funding for social services. Instead of that, it cut the funding by $340,000 to the provinces but it did not cut very expensive tax deductions.
The record of the government over a long time shows very specifically that the choices which would have helped the poor groups of people in this country have not been made. The choices made were those choices which allow the higher level of incomes to retain those earnings.
